speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I desire to ask a question of the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air. Will he give the house full information with respect to the recently reported incidents at Valleyfield?

speakeroldname: Hon. CYRUS MACMILLAN (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
subsubtopic: DISTURBANCE AT VALLEYFIELD ON JUNE 19
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon.
member for giving notice of his question. The A.O.C. of No. 3 training command reports that two men, one service and one civilian, were involved in a scuffle at 22:30 hours on the night of June 19 and were taken into protective custody by the local police. Subsequently a number of air force personnel appeared before the city gaol and requested the release of Sergeant Primeau, the airman involved, to which request the chief of police complied.
The full details of this are not entirely clear, but it appears that during the scuffle in the vicinity of the gaol a policeman received a blow, presumably from the fist of one of the service personnel present. His injuries, if any, were of a very minor nature and no hospitalization or medical treatment was necessary.
A court of inquiry was established ,and meanwhile all personnel, with the exception of a few who are living out, have been confined to barracks. The morning after the disturbance the usual route march was held, but these have been suspended by the A.O.C. in order not to excite any demonstrations. The A.O.C. stated that the newspaper reports were greatly exaggerated and that he has had conferences with the city manager and chief of police at Valleyfield, who are satisfied that everything possible is being done so that no further disturbances need be anticipated1. He has assured the civic authorities that any service personnel involved would be made available upon their request.	,
The A.O.C. has detailed two of the command legal officers to conduct the inquiry, and when the proceedings are received full details will be available and will be forwarded to air headquarters as quickly as possible. Squadron Leader Chopin was acting as commanding officer dtiring the absence of Wing Commander Cronyn on temporary duty. The latter has now returned to his station. There has apparently been a satisfactory end of the trouble, and there has been no further disturbance.

subsubtopic: FAR EAST-REPRESENTATIONS AND ARRANGEMENT RESPECTING FOOD, CLOTHING AND MEDICAL SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement respecting relief supplies to prisoners of war and internees in the far east.
On June 5 I promised the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) that I would make a statement about efforts which are being made to improve the position of prisoners of war in the far east.
In January last I outlined the attempts which had been made by the Canadian government and the Canadian Red Cross Society in collaboration with other allied governments and Red Cross societies, to establish a regular service for the sending of food, clothing and medicines to our nationals in the far east. For over two years now, continuous efforts have been made by the governments and Red Cross societies of the British commonwealth and the United States to secure Japanese agreement to the regular transmission of relief supplies. In spite of repeated disappointments, and rejection by the Japanese government of one proposal after another, we have persevered in our efforts. So far, only supplies carried by the exchange vessel Gripsholm and by the British exchange vessels during the course of civilian repatriation movements have reached allied nationals in Japanese and Japanese controlled territory. All possible supplies were carried by these ships, but the amount was pitifully small in relation to the needs of the thousands of prisoners of war and civilians in the far east.
In December of last year representatives of the British, American and Canadian Red Cross societies meeting in Washington appealed to the Japanese Red Cross to use their influence with the Japanese government and to offer advice and suggestions, with a view to establishing a regular service for relief supplies. More recently, through the agency of the Swiss government, the governments of the British commonwealth countries proposed to the Japanese government a plan for the regular shipment of food and medicines in both directions on a neutral ship under the auspices of the International Committee of the Red Cross and manned by a neutral crew plying regularly between an agreed allied port and a port on the perimeter of Japanese-controlled territory. This proposal is similar to one originally made by the Canadian government in 1942 but dropped then because other proposals seemed more likely to be accepted.
Prisoners oj War

The current plan provides that a 'second ship shall be placed at the disposal of the Japanese government to pick up the supplies at the entrepot and carry them to points where they are needed. This second neutral ship might be manned by a Japanese crew.
As yet no reply has been received from the Japanese government to this proposal, which was submitted to them by the Swiss government on May 8.
Some time ago, limited stocks of food, clothing and medical supplies were shipped jointly by the Canadian and American Red Cross societies to Vladivostok for onward transmission to allied prisoners of war and internees in Japanese hands. The Soviet government agreed to hold these supplies until an agreement was reached with the Japanese authorities for their movement and there are now fifteen hundred tons of relief goods stored in Vladivostok. On May 10 the United States government received a communication from the Japanese government, offering to send a ship to a Soviet port at regular intervals to pick up the relief supplies already stored at Vladivostok, as well as additional shipments of relief and mail which would be sent subsequently to Soviet territory. The Soviet government was consulted and they have indicated their willingness to have the stocks loaded on a Japanese ship at a convenient port near Vladivostok, or alternatively to send the supplies over land to be delivered to the Japanese authorities at a convenient border railroad station. The Soviet government has also offered the facilities of an equally accessible port, to which future shipments of supplies and mail may be sent. The Soviet proposals have been communicated to the Japanese government, and it is hoped that a regular service for relief supplies and mail for distribution to allied nationals in Japanese custody may be established.
All relief supplies sent to the far east under any of these plans would be pooled, that is, would be made available to Canadian and other commonwealth prisoners of war and internees, as well as to those of the United States and the Netherlands.
I wish to make it clear that the Swiss government as protecting power for Canadian and other British commonwealth interests in Japan is the official channel through which all formal approaches to the Japanese government are made. I have already, more than once, spoken of the gratitude we owe the Swiss for their untiring efforts on behalf of our prisoners and civilians in enemy hands. The cooperation of the Soviet government has been requested in this instance in view of the desirability of establishing a depot on

the pacific coast of the U.S.S.R. to which relief supplies can be forwarded and where they can be stored pending onward shipment to Japanese territory. The Canadian government, in common with the other interested governments, are deeply grateful to the Soviet government for their ready cooperation and willing assistance.

speechtext: I desire to ask a question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, arising out of a press item to the effect that for the first time in its history the wheat board has appointed a representative in Washington. Is the minister prepared to give a statement with regard to this change? Will he indicate also whether the reports appearing in some of the United States papers, to the effect that arrangements have been made whereby after the war the United States will buy a larger amount of Canadian wheat than anticipated, are correct?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO APPOINTMENT OP REPRESENTATIVE AT WASHINGTON
speechtext:
I am grateful to the hon. member for Lake Centre for giving me notice of his intention to ask these questions.
In answer to the first question, the Canadian wheat board has two principal considerations

Wheat Board
in appointing a representative in Washington. The first is that over the past eighteen months the United States has been purchasing very substantial quantities of feed grains from Canada, including wheat. For example, during the 1943-44 crop year to date the United States has imported 144,000,000 bushels of wheat, 62,000,000 bushels of oats, nearly 28,000,000 bushels of barley, nearly 9,000,000 bushels of rye and over 10,000,000 bushels of flaxseed. Altogether in the calendar year 1944 it is anticipated that the United States will import 170,000,000 bushels of Canadian wheat, in addition to what coarse grains are above our own requirements. Since the purchasing arrangements on wheat and the transportation on all grains have to be arranged between the Washington authorities and the Canadian wheat board, it will obviously be of advantage to the board to have a representative in Washington to serve as liaison between the board and the responsible Washington officials.
The second consideration is that Canada is an active participant in the operations of the combined food board, the cereals committee of which is bringing the grain supplies and requirements of the allied nations under international allocation. The cereals committee of the combined food board has been functioning since January of this year, with Mr. George Mclvor, chief commissioner of the Canadian wheat board, serving as its chairman. Since it is impossible for Mr. Mclvor to devote more than a small portion of his time to the work of this committee in Washington, the board's representative in Washington will be in a position to participate in the operations of the committee from day to day.
I might add that Mr. W. C. McNamara, who has been appointed to this position, has been associated with the Saskatchewan Pool Elevators Limited in Regina since 1924. More than two years ago he was lent to the Canadian wheat board and was in charge of the transportation department of the board. He has therefore been directly in touch with the transportation arrangements on the feed grain supplies which have already been moved to the United States.
I am sorry I am not in a position to-day to give the hon. member any information as to the supplies of wheat the United States may wish to buy in Canada next year. At the present time there does not appear to be any signs of a diminution in the demand from the United States.

speechtext: I was asked a question by the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) on Tuesday last about sugar for canning, and I promised to make a statement to-day. I dislike reading these long statements on the orders of the day, but I do not think there is any remedy for it.
It is important.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
maximum of twenty-five pounds of sugar per person available for canning purposes (only five pounds of which could be used for preserving jams, jellies and marmalade), ten pounds of this quantity being available through two coupons in each ration book and the remaining fifteen pounds being obtained [DOT] by application to local ration boards, indicating the quantities of fruits and preserves to be canned. Under this scheme United States consumers took up an average of only thirteen pounds of canning sugar per capita, and only approximately forty-five per cent of consumers made application for canning sugar beyond the ten pounds obtainable by ration book coupons.
Our experience in Canada was markedly different. In 1943 consumers were required to apply to their local ration boards for their full supply of canning sugar. While the wartime prices and trade board had anticipated that perhaps thirty-five per cent of tha population would make application, in actual fact eighty-four per cent of all consumers applied for an average of approximately twenty-three pounds of canning sugar per person. As this amount was just over double the amount of sugar which Canada had allocated for canning purposes or had previously used for this purpose, the solution which had to be adopted was to distribute through local ration boards an average amount of 11-3 pounds per applicant, the actual distribution of this amount in each district being left somewhat to the discretion of the local ration board to permit adjustment to local conditions. In addition, the introduction of the preserves ration in September made available, through the sugar alternative of the preserves ration, a maximum of an extra four pounds of sugar during the last four months of 1943, thus making it likely that consumers in Canada obtained on the average the thirteen pounds of sugar for canning which was the average in the United States.
Officials in the two countries are inclined to feel that the different results obtained in the two countries on the basis of somewhat similar policies are probably largely due to the fact that in many of the larger American cities an important section of the population does little or no home canning, with the result that on the average the supply of sugar for home canning has to be more widely distributed in Canada than in the United States. In any event, the experience of the United States authorities was such as to justify them in adopting for 1944 a policy very similar to that they had used in 1943. The only amendments made were those of detail; for example, only one coupon was included in ration books

to cover the acquisition of five pounds of canning sugar, application being required for the remaining twenty pounds this year as opposed to fifteen pounds last year, while consumers were relieved from the necessity of indicating this year in their applications how much fruit and preserves they proposed to put up. In addition, the five-pound restriction on sugar for jams, jellies and marmalade, a limitation which was never in effect in Canada, was removed. It should be noted that, although consumers may receive a maximum of twenty pounds of canning sugar on application, it lies within the discretion of local ration boards to reduce the amounts requested, and should, for instance, our own experience of last year be duplicated in the United States this year, this would become inevitable on a wide scale.
In Canada, on the other hand, our experience obviously indicated that a plan of this sort would be impracticable. Accordingly, it was decided to combine a standard allotment of ten pounds of canning sugar per consumer, to be available through special coupons in ration books, with a provision for supplementary quantities of sugar obtainable through the sugar alternative of the preserves coupon. This plan has the important advantage of providing the flexibility which is so desirable as between individual households, and of establishing an extremely equitable basis of distribution in that those households whose practice it is to do more home canning, and to purchase less in the way of commercially packed preserves, are able to do so by converting preserves coupons into sugar.
It is fully expected, in light of past experience, that this plan of dealing with the extremely difficult problem of canning sugar will prove to be satisfactory. Accordingly, and in view of the fact that there is no discrimination between Canadian consumers on one hand and American consumers on the other in the total amount of sugar being made available to them, there is no intention of amending the canning sugar distribution plans already announced.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this time our thoughts are overseas with the Canadian forces

Department of Reconstruction
who are fighting in a way that is worthy of their country and their cause. We look forward to the day when they will return, and we recognize that the very best welcome we can give them when they do return is that every one of them shall have employment in a job that will use his capacities to the full. The purpose of the department which this bill is to set up is to assist in creating opportunities for such employment, as well as to assist in coordinating the whole work of reconstruction.
I would have thought that such a bill introduced at this time might have received not only the support of all members but their support in speeches which did not raise political considerations. But on Tuesday night, when the debate began, there were one or two remarks made to which I think I should refer.
I refer particularly to remarks made by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in his speech in the house on Tuesday night. Towards the end of that speech he spoke as though he and his party wanted to see one single plan of reconstruction for the whole country. He spoke as though reconstruction was a tangible problem dealing with something concrete that could be dealt with in a single plan. He said at the end of his speech:
X was thinking of a plan for the whole country. A plan for all Canada would he more fitting than that.
Vv'e undoubtedly need plans for reconstruction, but no single plan will meet the needs of the Canadian people, of the Canadian provinces, of the Canadian municipalities, of Canadian industry, of Canadian agriculture, and of the government of the country as a whole. What we need is a complex of plans which will meet those needs. And we need more than that, We need an attitude towards the whole problem of reconstruction. We are not going to solve the problem by setting down a hard-and-fast blueprint, because we do not know what the conditions will be that we shall have to meet. We do not know when the war will end. We do not know how long the war against Japan will last, and naturally until we know those things we cannot set down the hard-and-fast lines of a plan. The whole problem is so complex and complicated that what is needed is a very flexible and resilient arrangement of devices, ideas and plans which will be ready to deal with the whole problem or with any part of the problem as it presents itself.
On that account we must regard the problem as complicated and difficult, and we are not going to meet it by saying that it is easy. We can provide full employment for all the people
of Canada and provide a maximum of income, but not by wishful thinking. It is not going to be met in that way. It can be met, but it is not going to be met by doing nothing about it, and it is the purpose of this department to coordinate the activities that must be carried on to do what is necessary when it is necessary to meet the problem.
Equally we cannot meet this problem by crying blue ruin and disaster, or by saying that after the war we are not going to have full employment, or that we are not going to be able to do this and that; and that, Mr. Speaker, is the attitude taken to a very considerable degree by the gentlemen opposite in the southwest comer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
I believe that I have
never interrupted anyone in the house, but I have always been willing to answer questions.
With regard to the question of the hon. member for Lethbridge, he has put that question three times in this debate; it has been answered three times; he has put it constantly to the house, and I do not think I should take up my time now in answering it any further. But I hope that my speech as it goes along will be an answer which he can accept, if he wishes.
The Minister of Finance in the speech which I have cited, referred to the objects at which we should aim and the paths we should take. I wish I had time to read extensively from this speech; it is magnificent. He ended with these words:
What I wish to emphasize to_ you to-day however is not the detailed direction in which we must advance, but rather that we must advance with the same vigour and energy after the war that we are now using in the war itself. We must pursue better housing with the same effort and effectiveness that we are devoting now to price control. We must conceive and carry out social insurance with the same boldness and thoroughness with which we have raised the income tax for war purposes. We must have the same courage and faith in financing useful peace-time development as we have had to apply in financing the war. We must retain the confidence that we have gained in the war, and shake off for ever the frustration which fell upon us in the 1930's.
I ask hon. members to contrast those two statements-the statement of Mr. Douglas, in which he said how many boys' lives it cost to get SI .20 a bushel for wheat, and referred to the certainty of unemployment under the present system, and the statement of the
Minister of Finance, in which he lays down aims and purposes and points the way that will be taken to achieve those aims. He, probably more than any man in Canada outside the Prime Minister himself, is by his service to the country demonstrating his capacity to carry out what he says he will do.
We are not going back after this war to 1939 or to 1932. We are not going back to any previous period. We are going forward on the basis of where we are at the end of the war, on the basis of 1944, 1945, 1946- whenever the war ends. I should like to call to the attention of hon. members that that starting point which we will have at the end of the war is a very different place and will find us in a very different situation from where we were even at the beginning of the war, and still less in 1932. The war has had an enormous effect on our productive capacity and on our skills. A country which can produce over 500 naval vessels and 200 ten thousand-ton boats, or 80,000 units of artillery and 10,000 planes, is a nation of considerable industrial capacity.
The London Economist, the leading British business paper, wrote:
Canada will emerge from the war one of the great industrial nations. She will be able to produce fifty per cent more iron and steel, five times as much aluminum, quantities of magnesium, tungsten, mercury and chromium. Her hydro-electric power capacity wrill be twenty per cent higher. She will have great shipyards, aeroplane factories, explosive and chemical plants, a synthetic rubber plant, armament factories, machine tool industries, instrument laboratories which were not here before the war. About one billion dollars has been spent in four years in additions to plant and equipment. There is a new industrial army of skilled men and women workers. A new tradition and a rich experience have been acquired.
What does this mean to people who are going to want jobs after the war? It means that provided we use these new capacities and these new skills we can produce jobs for everyone, jobs at wages that have never been known before.
Our position has improved in many other directions. Take wages, already the average weekly pay cheque of people engaged in manufacturing has gone up by almost fifty per cent. The national income has been doubled; about ninety per cent of the people of Canada are better off than *ver before; the external debt has been reduced; dividends have been reduced; salaries have been reduced, but wages income and security have gone up. The same thing is true of the position of the farmers. Despite a twenty-four per cent decrease in the number of people on the farms,
Department oj Reconstruction

the farmers of Canada are producing more than twice what they are doing before and they are getting twice as much as they got in 1939 for their produce. Agricultural production has doubled. The real purchasing power of the great majority of families in Canada is much higher than it has ever been, and to-day there are half a million more bank accounts than there were in 1939. Over seven million life insurance policies are in force, and three million Canadians bought war bonds in the last loan. The savings of individual men and women have increased by nearly four billions since the war.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: That is war time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Yes. But we are not going
to go back to the pre-war condition and stop everything just because my hon. friend says we are going to.
Now we can compare this situation with what it was in the last war. In the last war a few rich people became richer and poor people became poorer. That the exact contrary is true now is owing to the policies of the government and the support of the people of Canada during this war. In addition, there have been immense social gains in Canada owing to the way the war has been run. There has been a much better and fairer distribution of the national income, and there has been, in addition, unemployment insurance. To-day we heard read the notice to introduce a resolution to provide for family allowances on a scale not known in any other country in tihe world. That is part of the programme, and it is not a programme that will be put off until some far distant date. It is being carried out now while the war is on. My hon. friends can talk about the post-war period, but we are going to do in the way of social reform in Canada during the war the things that hon. gentlemen opposite talk about as part of their programme for the post-war period. We are going to begin the period of reconstruction very much better off not only than Canada has ever been before but probably better off than any other country in the world. We shall have greater natural resources. The record of achievement in the war, by our soldiers, workmen, industrialists, and farmers, is one that will make us proud to carry on after the war in the same splendid fashion as during hostilities.
The war has brought a change in the Canadian spirit, and that is something that we should recognize. No longer shall we be willing to face anything like the 1930's. We will not stand it, and there is no reason why we should. My friends opposite have fMr. Claxton.]
not a prerogative of that kind of talk, because nobody is going to stand it, and nobody is going to have, to stand it. It is not going to happen.
In this kind of discussion, very frequently, there creep in comparisons with the situation in other countries. As I said the other day in this house, it is unwise to make such comparisons unless for the purpose of emulation; but when these comparisons are made in a discussion of this kind invariably the person making the comparison picks out one single thing in respect of which some other country is better off and Canada has to match the best in the world. Well, usually Canada can match the best in all the world. But when we come to New Zealand particularly, a country for which I have the highest regard and where I have a great number of friends, I would suggest to my friends opposite that when they make comparisons they be fair and compare not only the scheme of social insurance, which is excellent in that country and which leads the world-there is no doubt about that-but also the standard of living, the standard of wages, national income, the burden of debt per . capita and the rate of interest that is payable on the debt of New Zealand. They should also compare the climates, soils and geographical situations of the two countries. If we are going to make comparisons, let us make a fair comparison and see where we stand and where they stand.
We cannot match every country with regard to everything, but we can say that there are few countries in the world which have so much of what is best as Canada has; and I ask my hon. friends, when they discuss the post-war situation here in comparison with other countries, to ask themselves frankly and honestly what country can offer more, where in the world can a young man such as any of our boys who are returning from overseas find better prospects for the future than in Canada?
We are going forward on the basis of where we shall be at the end of the war and not on the basis of where we were in 1932, and to do that we shall require a set of arrangements similar to, though not the same as, those that are necessary to conduct the war. The same kind of foresight, the same kind of cooperation, the same kind of coordination as are necessary in the conduct of the war will be needed for the mobilization of the resources of Canada, human and material, in the post-war period.
The problem of reconstruction has been usually considered under three heads. First is the rehabilitation and demobilization of the armed forces. On that, Canada's record is said by impartial observers to be the best in the world. We are said to have the most complete and comprehensive programme of

Department of Reconstruction
any in the world, a programme already working, not one to be carried out in the future, and that will improve steadily as discoveries and suggestions are made to that end.
But as I said in the opening of my remarks, the soldier's best welcome home is a job, and so the biggest part of our work in preparing for the post-war period must be to provide for industrial reconversion, and the provision of means of gainful employment for all our people who are willing and able to work.
This is going to be the greatest of all combined operations, and the new department will have the job of examining all plans and reports that have been made in order to provide maximum production, maximum employment, maximum income and maximum security. The department will look over all projects for public works and housing and fit them into a programme which can be put into action where it is necessary. It will involve close cooperation with industry, labour and the primary producers. It will involve the development of new industries, the extension of improvements gained during the war, the application of research, and the encouragement of initiative. The work already done in this field has been described by the Prime Minister. I have had an opportunity of examining it personally, and I can testify to the amount and the quality of the work of planning that has been done by the various interdepartmental committees that have been looking into this subject. ' That work will find its ultimate expression in government policy.
First comes the conversion of industry itself. Whether that industry be conducted by private enterprise or be publicly owned, the problems will be very much the same, and this question is receiving continuous consideration to-day under various heads, some of which I might mention.
Aids to production and cost reduction; tax and tariff reforms; expanded research; promotion of improved production and distribution methods; cheap credit, under which would come the Industrial Development bank, the National Housing Act, the agricultural credit bank, the central mortgage bank, amendments to the Bank Act, and the policies of the Bank of Canada; checks on inflation-because it is just as important in this post-war period that we do not let prices run away with us as it is to-day, and it may be more difficult then, so that we must consider what kind of controls will be needed to check inflation and distribute commodities in scarce supply. I should think the policy of this party, as opposed to that of some of the other parties, is to have the minimum amount of control necessary to do the job. Then there are improvements in
labour efficiency; expanded employment service; increased vocational and technical training facilities; effective grievance, arbitration and conciliation machinery, and the development and extension into the peace-time period of labour-management committees.
Then we come to the second main class of subjects receiving continuous consideration at the present time: the promotion and stabilization of markets. Under this come expanded foreign trade promotion services, which include reorganized trade commission service, machinery for greater coordination of departments and outside interests concerned with foreign trade; export credits-an export credit bill has been announced in the speech from the throne-and other similar subjects. To increase domestic consumption, which is part of the problem, we have the guaranteed floor prices announced in the speech from the throne; monetary policy; subsidies of various kinds as, for example, the subsidies to provide for guaranteed floor prices.
As part of the programme to increase consuming power and expand markets for Canadian goods, we have the social security programme, including the measure of which notice was given to-day, the family allowance legislation. This is a great step forward in the equalization and fair distribution of income, and at the same time a great humanitarian measure to provide a basic minimum for the family with children. It is one of the greatest and most daring financial and economic measures ever put forward in a democracy to increase the consuming and purchasing power of the whole community.
There is another class of subjects, Mr. Speaker, which must be considered and which is receiving continuous consideration; that is, the avoidance of obstacles to business. This means the removal of discriminatory and discouraging taxation, of the fear of direct governmental competition in various fields and, of course, measures to eliminate the domination of markets by cartels and monopolies.
All these matters are receiving consideration in various levels of the government departments to-day. The policies have been announced in the speech from the throne, and they will be amplified in good time, and in sufficient time.
From the field of industry, whether conducted privately or by public corporations, we come to the field of public improvements. This field usually holds first place in the minds of the people, and various parliamentary committees have given the matter a great
Department oj Reconstruction

deal of consideration. On Tuesday of this week the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) made a very interesting and constructive speech on this subject. This field may, if everything works out for the best, prove to be the least important in the long run, because if the economic and financial policies of the government are effective, and if we have a reasonable amount of international trade after the war, we will find that the programme of public improvements will not need to be nearly as extensive as some people now feel or fear. However, public improvements will be needed, and plans are being prepared. I can assure hon. members that hundreds of plans are now ready or in process of preparation, and the provinces and municipalities are similarly at work. What is required is that the work be coordinated, and then that questions of priority be settled.
All this great complex of questions involved in restoring our economy from a war-time to a peace-time basis can be carried out only with the united cooperation and good will of the Canadian people. It can also be carried out only by the cooperation of the dominion and the provinces, and for that purpose the dominion government has called a conference with the provinces, to be held just as soon as the convenience of all can be met. The purpose of that conference, and the attitude of the dominion at the conference, will be just this: that the ten governments concerned will sit down around a table to see what the postwar needs of the Canadian people are, how those needs can be met, and who can best do each part of the job.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: The blind leading the blind.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Well, the work already achieved in this field, as indicated in the Prime Minister's speech, would hardly indicate any great degree of blindness. I should think the reputation Canada has won for herself in the other countries of the world in the fields of economic and financial policy during the war, and the record of the Canadian people, would indicate that our policies will stand comparison with those of any other country in the world, and that they have led most other countries.
This conference between the dominion and the provinces will be of the utmost importance to the future of the people of Canada. I think it must be evident from the attitude taken so far by the dominion and the members of the government that the conference will not be entered into with any thought of endeavouring merely to secure the transfer of constitutional and financial power by one side or the other. The conference aims to see
fMr. Claxton.]
what is best for the people of Canada, how their needs can be met and who can best meet them; and if, as I expect, the provinces meet the dominion in that spirit, we can look forward to a satisfactory arrangement to deal with all these questions.
We cannot anticipate everything that lies ahead, but we can do a great deal. I can assure hon. members and the country at large that from what I have seen of the work of the economic advisory committee, of the various inter-departmental committees, and of the committee in preparation for the dominion-provincial conference, these questions, which are of the utmost concern to all members, to all people in Canada and to our boys and girls in the armed forces, are receiving consideration every day of the week by about as able a group of servants any people or any government in the world can boast.
We can help them. Various parliamentary committees have been of enormous help, as have also the voluntary associations, committees and agencies of different kinds which have forwarded briefs. There are literally hundreds of plans for post-war reconstruction and development available. It will be the task of the new minister to coordinate all those activities and to draw them together in what I have described as the greatest combined operation-next to the war-in the history of the people of Canada. I am confident we can meet the challenge in a way which will justify the opportunities given to us by our being privileged to live in this great and glorious country.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I followed with much interest the speech of the hon. member who has just taken his seat. I shall not discuss any of his arguments, but I was amused when at the outset of his speech he appeared to banter across the floor with members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party. It has occurred to me that there might be considerable jealousy between the government and the C.C.F. We have always been told that the C.C.F. was the party of the left, and that they were travelling on the left side of the road. If we follow the legislation offered by the present government for some time past it seems to me the public might be justified in concluding that the government is jockeying with the C.C.F. for this particular position.
An hon. member who spoke a few days ago said that the Liberal party was following the middle of the road. As all hon. members know, that is a dangerous position. However, they may have been on the right side of the road at one time and crossed over to the middle. At the moment however they are

Department of Reconstruction
now crowding the ditch on the left side of the road, and if we can believe indications I am satisfied they will soon be in the ditch.
It is not my intention to analyse the bill at length. Opportunity will be afforded in committee, when the bill is considered section by section; so that I shall content myself with making a few remarks in respect of its general application.
I am sure all hon. members approve the government's action in setting up a Department of Reconstruction. It is a necessity; and any government in power at the present time would have had to follow a similar procedure. Not only is it a necessity in Canada, but in this war-tom world I am satisfied every country will have to set up departments of reconstruction, or take other steps to build up their worn-out industries.
A few days ago the Prime Minister (Mr Mackenzie King) said that he had no idea how long the war in Europe would last. He also said that when the war was over it would be necessary for us to operate against Japan. I believe that all hon. members will agree heartily with those statements. He pointed out, however, that reconstruction, because of its tremendous implications, could not be left until the close of the war. We know as a matter of fact that many men have already been demobilized in Canada. Those men must be rehabilitated in civil life, and we must also make our plans so that we can look after the men who are coming home, look after those who are engaged in the manufacture of munitions, and in general look after the problems of the country in years to come.
Some speakers have pointed out that the responsibility rests with all governing bodies, and with that statement I agree. Our federal government, our municipal governments, even governments of towns and villages, including all the individuals of which they are composed, are interested in matters of reconstruction, and all must bear their share of the responsibility.
As the last speaker (Mr. Claxton) said, we are fortunate in Canada in having great natural resources. No party, of course, can claim credit for those resources; they are our great, God-given heritage. But it is up to our government and to us as individuals to see that those resources are used to the very best advantage. We have great agricultural lands, extending from one end of Canada to the other, and capable of yielding abundant crops of all kinds. We have great mineral deposits in the far north capable of producing untold wealth. Our waters teem with fish, and we have more than three-quarters of a million square miles of productive forest lands. In
addition to these we have harnessed much of our water-power for the production of electrical energy, and there is great potential capacity still unharnessed. Nature has indeed been more than kind to us, and if, as other hon. members have said, any country can formulate policies for reconstruction and the employment of its people, certainly that country should be Canada.
But it is not enough to possess these great resources. We shall benefit from them only as we learn to develop them directing what is necessary of the finished products to our own use, and trading the surplus in other parts of the world.
When he spoke the other day the Prime
Minister said:
We shall do well, I believe, -to bear in mind that prosperity is indivisible. It is not something which one nation can have and enjoy by itself; it is something that has to be shared. We shall have to come to see that we are members one of another and that no nation liveth unto itself.
That is a statement with which all can agree; there can be no prosperity in the world unless every nation is prosperous. I believe one hon. member has said that in point of air travel we are within sixty hours of any other spot on the face of the earth. No doubt that time will be still further contracted as the aeroplane becomes faster and faster, and as time goes on. As no nation can be prosperous unless all other nations are prosperous, so in Canada no part can be prosperous unless every other section prospers. We can go farther and say that no industry can be prosperous unless other industries prosper, and that no city or town can prosper unless the people throughout the country and in the farming districts also prosper.
I believe I may be pardoned if in my brief observations this afternoon I refer to some of the problems facing the people in the maritime provinces. I would ask hon. members to consider some of our primary industries, and how a process of reconstruction may be applied to them. Let us first consider the fishing industry. Some of us live by the sea, and many of our people are engaged in that great industry, one which is widely diversified. In the maritime provinces we have over 2,000 miles of coast line, and there are many thousands of square miles in which fishing operations are conducted. Over thirty thousand fishermen are employed in the industry. They, with their families, constitute about one-sixth of the population in the maritime provinces.
We have many varieties of edible fish. I think it can be truthfully said that the finest fish anywhere in the world are caught in the waters in and around the three maritime
Department oj Reconstruction

provinces. About seventy-nine per cent in value of the catch in those provinces is taken not by the offshore fishermen, as they are called, but by the inshore fishermen. That means they are caught by the individual fisherman, and it becomes the livelihood of the small man, or the man who goes out in his own boat and does his own fishing and does not depend upon trawlers or some other larger means of catching fish.
From 1923 to 1939 the fishing industry in those provinces was in a very poor condition. It was in a state of depression. The average earnings of a fisherman were estimated at that time to be $244 per year, not including operating expenses. The situation became so bad that, as hon. members will remember, one of the great daily papers of the maritime provinces, the Halifax Herald, decided to make an investigation. They sent one of the members of the press gallery here, Mrs. Tufts, to investigate the situation. I think that all hon. members are familiar with the excellent report that was made by Mrs. Tufts. In 1932 the price of fish to the fishermen was one cent per pound. I do not think any more need be said to call the attention of the house to the deplorable conditions affecting any group of men who would have to accept a price like that. In 1939 it had risen to one and three-quarter cents a pound.
The hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Hill) said on Tuesday last that a floor had been put under the price of fish. That is true, but it was done by the price control board as a war measure. What I wish to emphasize to the house is that after the war in the reconstruction period a floor price must also be put under the price of fish if the fishing industry is to be maintained in those small provinces.
A number of other things were recommended by the fishermen of the maritime provinces in the brief which was submitted to the reconstruction committee. I wish to support in every way possible these recommendations. One of them was that freezing plants and cold storage plants be located at strategic points along the coasts of the different provinces. If that were done it would be of great benefit -and I might point out that it could well become a public utility. The fishermen have suffered in the past because of a lack of many facilities for catching, freezing and marketing of their fish. There is no reason why, in the days of reconstruction, this great body of our inhabitants should not receive the consideration which has been withheld from them so long.
There is also the matter of transportation. I am not going to deal with these points particularly, but I should like to bring them to

the attention of the house. These fish are perishable, as everyone knows, and facilities for transporting them must be provided so that they may get to the different markets in good condition. I do not know whether it is feasible or not, but it seems to me that aeroplanes could be utilized for that purpose. We read of thousands of men being transported to France in great air liners. It is possible in fhe days to come that the fishing industry can be greatly helped by exporting fish from the maritime provinces by aeroplane to the different markets in Canada. It may also be possible to do it by glider plane, in order that the people of the central provinces and other parts of Canada may have the benefit of the fresh fish of the maritimes.
One of the other great resources of our country is our forests. More than ninety per cent of the forest areas are owned by the crown. By that I do not mean to say they are owned by the Dominion of Canada, but they are owned in the right of the provinces and the dominion. This great asset has been greatly neglected in the past. When I came back from overseas after the last war someone pointed out to me the terrible waste in the forests of our land. I also had the opportunity, as did most men who were overseas, of visiting the forests of England and France, and of making a comparison between the care given them in Europe and in Canada. The lack of care that we have given them in Canada is something that would, I am sure, appal hon. gentlemen. I have walked through the forests in England and in France. You would not find in those forests a small piece of wood the size of your finger. Everything is conserved and gathered up. Underbrush is cleared away. The forests are protected in every way. In this country we have been most neglectful. It is still true that for every hundred thousand feet of timber cut an additional forty thousand feet is lost through fire. Insects and disease destroy another large portion. There has been and still is waste everywhere in the forests of this country. In the past-this has been debated before in this house, but since it is so important I see no harm in again calling attention to it-the dominion parliament has not taken a vital interest in the matter. It has not realized the great asset we have in the forests of the country. I contend that in the reconstruction period no finer work could be done by the reconstruction department now being set up than the conservation, protection and care of the great forests of Canada.
In my own province we depend largely on the forests. Over eighty per cent of the twenty-eight thousand square miles of New

Department of Reconstruction
Brunswick is still unsettled. It is made up of forest and woodlands to a great extent: For the year 1943 the estimated value of the forest products of New Brunswick totalled $56,000,000. This figure included the value of 300,000,000 board feet of sawn lumber; 823,000 cords of pulpwood used in the six pulp and paper mills in the province; 464,000 cords sold outside, and nearly a million cords of firewood-a product of great importance in the present national fuel emergency. Therefore everyone can see what a valuable asset the forests are not only to Canada, but to the small provinces, and to New Brunswick in particular.
I have read the report of the subcommittee on agricultural policy. I do not intend this afternoon to make any extended remarks -with regard to it, but I agree in large measure with all the recommendations that have been made. I suggest that when the department is set up the recommendations of the committee on agricultural policy be implemented.
In New Brunswick we are interested not *only in fishing and forestry as primary industries. Agriculture is a great industry. Any one who has visited New Brunswick and has gone down the Saint John river must have realized that it is one of the finest farming districts of Canada. He would also find the same splendid farms up the Kennebecasis river, over through the Annapolis valley, and in other parts of Nova Scotia and in practically all of Prince Edward Island. Close .attention must be paid by the reconstruction *committee to the position of the farmers in the three maritime provinces. To-day our farms can produce. During the war we have produced, with a limited number of men to work on the farms, far more agricultural products than we did in pre-war days. To give hon. gentlemen an idea of our production, in 1942 and 1943 we had the largest crops in the history of the province; and they were produced, I would point out, with many thousands of our young men overseas, with worn-out machinery, and with the people at home having to work very long hours. Our production of butter was 7,000,000 pounds in 1942, an increase of forty per cent; and I am very proud to say that in my home town *of Sussex there is a butter factory which produced more butter in one month in 1943 -than any other butter factory in the whole Dominion of Canada. But we have our handicaps and they constitute one of the problems which must be considered by the reconstruction committee.
One of the handicaps of the farmers of the maritime provinces has been high freight
rates, and another the lack of markets. The question of freight rates has been discussed in this house on a good many occasions, and it would not be fair for me to take up time in dealing with it now. But it is a question that should engage the attention of the reconstruction committee, because high freight rates have a detrimental effect upon the provinces down by the sea. The cost of feed, for instance in New Brunswick is much higher than it is in Ontario, Quebec and the western provinces, with the result that the farmers of the maritimes who wish to raise hogs start under a severe handicap and it is impossible for them to compete in the bacon market in England with farmers from other parts. The same thing applies to fertilizer, which all farmers now use. We in the maritime provinces pay about one dollar per ton more for certain types of fertilizer than do the farmers in Quebec and other provinces. These are conditions, Mr. Speaker, which I contend must be corrected if we are to have the people in all parts of this dominion treated in the same manner, as I feel it is only just and right they should be treated.
Speaking of transportation, I do not think it is out of the way to bring to the attention of the house a transportation project which is not new so far as New Brunswick and Nova Scotia are concerned, and not new so far as the federal government is concerned. I refer to the Chignecto canal. The construction of a canal between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia was first thought of nearly three hundred years ago, when the French government was in control of Acadia, as it was then called; the French governor in 1686 recommended it to the French government as an undertaking which should be carried out at that time. He said that the Northumberland strait should be connected up with the bay of Fundy. .Representations have been repeatedly made over a long period of years to the federal government that this canal should be constructed, because, it was pointed out, it would be of great benefit to the people in that part of the dominion. But in spite of the fact that, not millions, but hundreds of millions of dollars have been spent on the building of canals in other parts of this dominion, we have never been able to get what I believe to be this very necessary Chignecto canal, which -would be a tremendous asset to us in that part of the country.
To show some of the advantages there would be in constructing this canal, I point out that the distance between Charlottetown and Saint John over the route that we have to travel at the present time is 488 miles; if the Chignecto canal were cut, the distance would be 144
Department oj Reconstruction

miles. From Dalhousie to Saint John is now 720 miles; via the Chignecto canal it would 360 miles. From Pictou to Saint John is now 4S0 miles; via the Chignecto canal it would be 170 miles. From Montreal to Saint John is now 1.379 miles; via the Chignecto canal it would be 1,104 miles. From Montreal to Windsor, Nova Scotia, is now 1,250 miles; via the Chignecto canal it would be 820 miles. From Montreal to Hillsborough, New Brunswick, is now 1,235 miles; via the Chignecto canal it would be 760 miles. The saving in mileage and in the cost of transportation between the centres of upper Canada and the maritimes would be very great. The construction of this canal would be of benefit not only to our primary producers in the maritime provinces but also in reducing the cost of goods that we have to purchase from other parts of Canada. Besides, in these times when we are speaking of public works that must be carried on in order to provide employment when our men come back from overseas, I would point out that no public work could be carried on which would be of more benefit to the people of the maritime provinces and give better employment to the returned men than this construction. It would help all the industries of the maritime provinces. It would help our fishing industry; it would help our farmers and our manufacturers, and be of benefit to the people generally.
There is not much that I can say, Mr. Speaker, about the industries of the maritime provinces, because we have so very few of them. We have suffered much from a lack of industries in the past.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
You should have more
industries.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
We have heard that for a long time. It is true that we should have more, and I believe that we will have more. Some seventy-five years ago we did have good industries in the maritime provinces, industries in nearly every city and town, but then the tendency towards centralization began and our industries were moved to Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton and other large centres in the central provinces. When I spoke in the house in the month of March last I pointed out what a detrimental effect this moving away of our industries has had on the economic position of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. It meant the draining away of our people in the maritime provinces. There are more people to-day in the New England states who are descendants of people in the maritime provinces than there are in our own province. Why? Because we have not large industries in the maritime provinces

to keep them there. And so, Mr. Speaker, when this new department is functioning I trust that it will consider well the decentralization of industry and take steps to provide more industries for the small provinces down by the sea.
We are told that one reason we have not more industries in the maritime provinces is that we have not electric power. That possibly has been true during this war. But no great effort has been made by the dominion government to provide electric power for the maritimes. The project is now being mooted- I am not an engineer and cannot speak as to its feasibility-of the development of the Petitcodiac river in Westmorland county in New Brunswick. From what I have heard I should think it is a practicable proposition. If the Petitcodiac river were developed it would mean the electrification of the farms of practically all Prince Edward Island. It would mean the electrification of farms and industry in the southern part of New Brunswick. It would mean electrification and the providing of power to industry in other sections of Nova Scotia. This, I contend, must commend itself very seriously to any government or department which is set up to deal with reconstruction.
Perhaps it has taken this great war to awaken Canadians to the responsibility which one section of the country has to another. We in the maritimes have entertained thousands of young men from all parts of Canada. Men from western Canada have been amazed at the beauty of our scenery, the fertility of our soil, and the great potentialities which our section of Canada possesses. I believe that with the information they have obtained, when the war is over our requirements will receive more sympathetic attention than they have had in the past. What is true of the men coming from the west is true also of the regiments who have gone from the east to western Canada; they are getting an idea of the problems which face western people. I believe that this increase and exchange of knowledge will have splendid results; it will lead to better understanding and a more united Canada.
I notice that section 6, which defines the powers of the minister, states:
The minister, to enable him to perform the duties imposed upon him by this act, may:
(c)	consult with representatives of primary producers, industry, science and labour upon any question connected with reconstruction.
That is all to the good. He also has the power to-
(d)	establish committees or boards and use existing organizations and agencies to assist him in carrying out the purposes of this act.

Department oj Reconstruction
I trust that on these committees and boards all sections of this country, all political parties and various forms of industry will be represented. The problem is so big that every section, every view, every opinion should be well canvassed and considered, so that no part of the country shall be left unrepresented and all parts shall receive the attention to which they are entitled.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
This is a bill which no hon. member can afford to oppose. It is an effort to set up now a department of reconstruction in order that when we pass from war to peace-which we all hope will be soon, and which, on the deliverance of the Prime Minister of Great Britain not long ago, we have good reason to hope may not be long deferred-the problems which may then arise will find us prepared.
Before I deal with two or three phases of the matter I wish to recall some of the statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in introducing this bill, two days ago. He pointed out that the new department will be primarily concerned with economic reconstruction, and with that observation I fully agree. The reform of our economic policy, in my view, stands at the threshold of all our future efforts for reconstruction. He also indicated that almost every department of government will have some special work to do. That also is very true. But you can forget the efforts of the other departments of government if you do not provide them, through the finance department, with the necessary means to carry out a policy of reconstruction.
The Prime Minister intimated that the new minister's duties will be carried out in cooperation with his colleagues of other government departments, and I suggest to the house that the first and second and third steps to seek cooperation in his plans will be from the finance department.
We have been told that an advisory committee on economic policy, under Mr. W. C. Clark, have been studying this problem since January 23, 1941; and the Prime Minister told us also:
There have been discussions on economic matters.
I quote him exactly, from Hansard, page 3986:
I cannot say how successful they may be.
He further told the house, as reported on page 3988:
I do not think my hon. friend need fear about the increase of the public debt or taxation to accomplish these things. ... I believe the
nation can go ahead with the great work of construction and reconstruction and at the same time reduce its taxation and reduce its debt.	.
That is bold and hopeful and optimistic language, and I desire to endorse that hopeful prediction of the future. I do not think I can give my viewpoint as to how it shall be done better than to quote his own language, as reported in Hansard in 1933, reiterated in 1934, when he said, with regard to the necessary economic policy of this country, as reported in Hansard of that year at page 4365:
Once a nation parts with the control of its currency and credit it matters not who makes the nation's laws. Usury, once in control, will wreck any nation. Until the control of the issue of currency and credit is restored to government and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of the sovereignty of .parliament and of democracy is idle and futile.
In 1933, the Prime Minister, as reported in Hansard of that year at page 2511, uttered this great policy, enunciated on behalf of the Liberal party who constitute the government of to-day:
The Liberal party belfeves that credit is a public matter, not of interest to .bankers only, -but of direct concern to the average citizen. It stands for the immediate establishment of a properly constituted national central bank to perform the functions of rediscount, and the control of currency issue, considered in terms of public need. A central bank is necessary to determine the supply of currency in relation to the domestic, social and industrial requirements of the Canadian people and also to deal with the problems of international commerce and exchange.
I desire to direct special attention to these words:
. . . a properly constituted national central bank to perform the functions of rediscount, and the control of currency issue, considered in terms of public need.
Note "in terms of .public need", not possible private gain.
I am compelled to believe that that splendid enunciation of policy has been carried out in part, but in part only. We have since then established a wholly owned national bank, the Bank of Canada. But I ask the members of this house whether we have taken steps to see that the control of currency, and the issue of currency, has been made on the credit of the nation in accordance with public need, or whether, on the contrary, it passed over into private hands, the hands of the chartered or private bankers of the country.
Let me make this suggestion, and I make my suggestions in a desire to be helpful to the Prime Minister and to the government and to lay before parliament what I believe to be the duty of this parliament at this session, here
Department oj Reconstruction

and now, and not to be left to the hands of a minister of reconstruction and his staff one or two years from now, no matter how eminent or industrious he may be. The minister under this bill has not a chance in the world to carry out the high purpose of the Prime Minister unless we in this parliament give him, at this session in this parliament and not at some time in the dim, distant future, the economic power to do so. I wish to make some suggestions which I regard as essential if this bill is truly to serve the Canadian people. The chart to be followed has been laid down in the language I have read to the house, but if we have put it into effect only in part, now is the time to round it out, to complete it at this session of parliament, in order that the relief we all desire the people to have may become an accomplished fact.
I have very strong views, Mr. Speaker, which I have not attempted to secrete, with regard to the subject of taxation and public borrowing, which the Prime Minister has placed before the house as one of the objectives to be accomplished by this new department. Let me say that our first consideration must never be lost sight of in this parliament. There must be no slackening in our war effort. There must be no legislation, no economic policy laid down which could in the slightest way prevent our country from seeing to it that our army and our allies have Canada at their back 100 per cent, to the fullest possible degree in the prosecution of this war, until unconditional surrender is forced upon our enemies. But having full regard to that, sir, we can and should look forward now, with quickening vision, because that is what this bill purports to do, to the reduction of taxation particularly as it affects the farmer, the lumberman, the settler, the fisherman, the industrial workers and those who through no fault of their own have the most difficulty in the struggle for existence. Let me give the house some details of the specific relief which I advocate putting into effect now, and which I have pressed upon the government, and desire in the most friendly way to continue to press upon the government and upon parliament, upon every member of this house.
It is time to sink some political differences and lend oursedtves to this grave and difficult problem of reconstruction. That is what this bill lays the foundation, or purports to lay the foundation, to do. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to my fellow members that this parliament should reduce at once the taxation on unmarried men and women in the lowest brackets by raising the exemption from $660 a year to $1,200 a year, so that no man or
[Mr. Slaghto
woman who earns less than $100 a month should pay any income tax at all. They will continue to pay the sales tax; they will continue to pay the amusement tax; they will continue to pay a multiplicity of other indirect taxes on everything they eat and buy and wear and attempt to put into their houses. That will mean a los of revenue, through personal income tax, of $32 million and no more, but it will bring relief to 300,000 Canadian men and women. Second, I suggest that it is the duty of parliament to increase the exemptions for married people from the present $1,200 a year to $1,800 a year, so that no married person shall be called upon to pay income tax at all unless they receive at least $150 a month. That will mean a relief, on the basis of last year's collections, to 650,000 people, and it will create a loss of revenue to the treasury of only $55 million.
The result of these two changes will be to free altogether from income tax 950,000 Canadians who are least able to pay, whose struggle to make ends meet is the most difficult, and most of whose taxes are taken from them, before they ever reach their pockets, by their employers under the rigid method now in vogue known as deduction at the source. The total loss in revenue by giving a breathing spell to 950,000 of our people is therefore only $87 million out of a total revenue, taxed and borrowed, of five and a half billion dollars to be spent this year by a country of eleven and a half million people.
It is my belief that in times of heavy taxation those best able to pay should be called upon before we hit those least able to pay, and through no fault of their own. I further contend that we should reduce the present rate of personal income tax on everybody's taxes by a reduction of twenty-five per cent, or one quarter of the present personal income tax. By so doing we would incur a further loss in revenue of $220 million, being one quarter of the present total taxes collected from personal income last year. I go farther and insist, so far as my voice can insist, that the excess profits tax, which is paralyzing the small business man and which is going far to strangle all business in Canada, should be reduced at once by twenty-five percent, and that in the first year after the war a further reduction of another twenty-five per cent at least should be made. That means a further loss in revenue of $137,500,000. Those versed in arithmetic who may have followed me will find that I have indicated a policy which will mean a total loss of revenue, from the four items I have described, of $434,500,000, and you, Mr. Speaker, may very properly ask, "How shall we make that up if we do give our

Department of Reconstruction
anything about money, but I do know that the municipalities in British Columbia cannot possibly take their proper share in the reconstruction programme unless they get assistance from the federal treasury.
Another thing in which I do not agree with the Prime Minister is that he has not much fear, as I understood him the other day, of the immediate six months following the peace. Personally I think that the first six months following the peace are going to present a very serious problem. Possibly I am looking at it from the soldier's point of view. I do not think you are going to be able to keep the men in the army after the war. The men will look after that themselves. The desire of every soldier will be to get home as quickly as he can and to get out of uniform, with the possible exception of the air force. These men are going to be thrown on to the labour market immediately after peace is declared. They will have a certain amount of deferred pay, which was an excellent idea on the part of the department, and a certain amount of savings. But I hope that every young soldier coming back from the war will not make the same mistake that I made and that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) made. I waited twenty years after the war before I got married. I hope these young soldiers will get married immediately, but I do not know how far their savings will carry them if they get married unless we have concrete plans ready for their employment when they return. So far as I know, no concrete plans have been made by the government and no blue-prints prepared to put these men to work immediately after peace is declared. If peace were declared next week, the federal government, so far as I know, has no plans complete as yet to put these men and women immediately to work. We have had a wonderful reconstruction committee which has studied and submitted various plans.
I will tell you how we do it in British Columbia. The government of the day in British Columbia set up a committee, not of the government, but of the legislature, and that committee toured every little district in the province and got ideas from the Canadian Legion, from boards of trade, women's institutes, municipalities, and every other organization they could think of, as well as from individuals. I want to tell you that I am proud of the fact that I come from the province of British Columbia because within one week after peace is declared the British Columbia government can call for contracts for $10,000,000 worth of constructive work. That is a wonderful record. I want hon.
gentlemen to mark that. I do not know how it is in the other provinces, and I am not criticizing them. So far as I know the federal government has no plans ready with which they can proceed to put men to work immediately after peace is declared. They have suggested various ideas-public buildings, waterways, railway expansion, and so on. But I repeat that British Columbia, through its Department of Public Works and other departments, has blueprints already prepared and estimates already made so that within one week after peace is declared they can call for tenders of $10,000,090 of constructive work. I think that that is the attitude which the federal government should adopt. I may be wrong; the federal government may have its plans ready, but if they are ready, this house has never been told about any concrete plans.
There is another matter. But first I had better continue with the Prime Minister, because there are some other things on which I do not agree with him, and if you are going to disagree I think it is a good idea to disagree from the top down, starting with your leader. I am not going to speak in a sobbing voice and then stab him in the back unless I decide to move across the floor o<n the same day.
One thing in which I am particularly interested so far as the soldiers are concerned is farming. I should like to quote what was said by the chairman of the reconstruction committee, the man who I think is most intimately connected with the reconstruction programme next to the Prime Minister himself. We are very glad that he comes from British Columbia. He and his committee have done an excellent job, and I am sorry that the chairman is not here to-day. He happens to be in hospital, and I know that I speak for every member when I wish him a speedy recovery. I quote in part what he said with respect to food at page 3994 of Hansard of June 20 of this year:
In this respect we welcome the conclusion arising from the united nations food conference that never again-
I repeat that.
-that never again will food :be destroyed simply because people have not enough money to buy it.
That is from the chairman of the reconstruction committee. I point that out because I want to speak of it in connection with the Veterans' Land Act. Coming from the chairman of the committee it may be presumed that he was speaking for the government. What notice are we giving to the boys overseas with respect to this matter at the present time? Are we telling them that we in this parliament are not going to permit the

Department oj Reconstruction

destruction of food in this country? Hon. members will recall that the great president of the country to the south made [DOT] probably the only mistake he has ever made in his leadership when he allowed brood sows to be destroyed. Brazil also destroyed coffee. Here we state through the chairman of the reconstruction committee that never again will food be destroyed simply for lack of money. Actually what do we find in Canada to-day? We in parliament are not supreme. What is going on in Manitoba? I quote this from the Winnipeg Tribune:	"Growers plough under
Manitoba Strawberries." I quote this because the soldiers of Manitoba will scarcely think us sincere in our plans for reconstruction, particularly as regards agriculture, when they see that we permit a few bureaucrats to allow this sort of thing to go on. There is a picture in this same paper of strawberries being ploughed under by a tractor, and under the picture is this:
Goodbye, Strawberries: Strawberry growers near Winnipeg are ploughing under their strawberries, as Aleida Daman, 18, daughter of Peter Daman, St. Vital grower, is doing in this picture. The prices 'board set too low a ceiling for berries, they say, and growers see no sense in paying labour $4.50 a day to keep the bushes in shape.
That must be an extensive piece of ground to have a tractor ploughing under this food. This paper is going to the soldiers of Manitoba who are over there in Italy and on the shores of France. Yet at the same time we are telling them we shall never let the lack of money cause the destruction of food. It will take more explanation from the government than I have heard yet to convince the boys over there that that policy is being carried out when they see food being destroyed in this way.
The reason I refer to this matter particularly is that in British Columbia we have some 750 Japanese farms which were all producing berry farms before we seized them-no, we did not seize them; we were too generous; we bought them out. We are holding these farms for soldiers when they come back. What will our soldiers in Italy or on the shores of France think of our Veterans' Land Act when in British Columbia out of 171 farms 121 have been allowed to go to wrack and ruin, and the people on the remainder axe producing at a loss to-day simply because of the dictates of the almighty dollar, orthodox finance and the war prices board?
We estimate that we have over 300,000 acres of land now surveyed and available, and on which soil analyses have been taken. The provincial government are prepared to grant

a million acres of land to the men who are coming back. But all we are going to allow a man who wants to go on the land is $4,800 to buy a farm and $1,200 for the purchase of stock to equip that farm.
