equipment. Therefore the farmer is entitled to exactly the same consideration in any adjustments respecting income tax.
I hope that the budget is not quite completed. I happen to have my office on the fifth floor, and as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) is located on the same floor, there is a continuous stream going and coming. I wish they would come in to me for advice in preparing the budget. I was quite flattered about something which happened yesterday. My office is in about the centre of the block. One of the most popular and esteemed members of the cabinet has his office on the fourth floor immediately below mine. Inadvertently yesterday he opened the door of my office and walked in, and he said, "Goodness, I must have opened the wrong door." I said, "No, it is all right." I will not tell you his name; it begins with a C. Coming events cast their shadows before; it may be that he came in to look over my office before I move down to his. Seriously, I hope the Prime Minister takes into consideration this important fact that agriculture is just as much entitled as any other industry to money for reconversion. The farmer is in the same position as the industrialist'. He needs new binders, new tractors, other new equipment, and he should have the same consideration in so far as income tax is concerned.
There is one thing to which, I think, not enough attention has been paid. I want to congratulate the leader of the opposition (Mr. Gray don), who made, I thought, an excellent address yesterday. Particularly I would like to compliment the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), who, I believe, is the only member who in the course of this discussion has touched on education, although it is a factor in reconstruction which affects the entire dominion and one in which, I think, we all should be interested. His speech last evening was very fair and very constructive. It is not often, possibly, that I can say that. I wish I could say the same for the leader of his party, who goes around and makes strange statements, probably for vote-catching purposes, about what he thinks the soldiers want. If anybody stops to think, he will know that what the expression "the Canada he left" means is that the soldier wants to get back-to the Canada he left, to peace-loving Canada, and particularly, his mother's cooking. The speech of the hon. member for York South, however, was helpful, and I congratulate him, and also the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), who is always interesting.
I do not want to take any more time, except to impress upon the government that we in
Department oj Reconstruction

British Columbia will not be satisfied with a dollars and cents approach to this matter. After the announcement made by the Prime Minister to-day I do not know how any member of this house or anybody else in Canada can think in terms of dollars and cents about what is to be given as a matter of right to Canadian men and women coming back from the war. Money must never be allowed to stand in the way of what we are going to do for those men and women, and I urge upon the government that representation of the soldiers and of the women serving in the forces should be considered in the setting up of these boards under the reconstruction department-above all, the women. Little has been said about the way in which we are going to deal with the women coming back to civilian life from the army and from war industry. That will be one of the greatest problems we shall have to tackle. Money will not always provide the solution so far as the women are concerned. With money you can always find work for men, but you cannot always find suitable work for women, no matter how much money you may have. I suggest therefore that the government would be well advised in the setting up of these boards to consider the representation of the women in the armed services. The government might take representatives from the women's institutes and from those serving in the armed forces, as well as representatives who will look after the interests of the men in the army.
I am a party member, but I say that if the government sincerely wishes this department to be a success, politics in any form must be kept out of it. If anything is to be kept out of the department it is politics. Irrespective of party we should initiate a programme that has been planned for the good of all and not for the advantage of the few.

speechtext:
Before addressing a few remarks to the points I intended to cover in this debate, I hope my hon. friend who just preceded me (Mr. Cruickshank) will not take offence if I attempt to give him the other side of the story in regard to the Veterans' Land Act. I wish to suggest seriously to him that he should add up the over-all benefits which the new Veterans' Land Act proposes to give to the returned man who might wish to go farming. If he does so, perhaps he will revise his views in this connection. If he will add up all the benefits, he will find that the dominion government is making a cash grant substantially close to $3,000 to every Canadian veteran fMr. Cruickshank.]
who. wants to go farming under the Veterans' Land Act.
Before discussing that, I might add that any boy who will make a good farmer will in my opinion be entirely successful if he starts with $3,000 cash assistance and when the balance of his liability carries interest at a rate of only 3^ per cent. In adding up these benefits we find the veterans' initial responsibility is to pay $480 down in cash. The government, on the other hand, makes a cash contribution of $2,320 of the purchase price, $1,120 on account of the farm and $1,200 for implements, in addition to supplying the finances. That is made up in this way. As regards stock and implements, if the fanner is successful he pays nothing for the stock and implements; that is $1,200 of the amount I have referred to. The criticism is that $1,200 is not an adequate amount to equip a farm with stock and implements. Well, I suggest that it was never the intention that $1,200 should fully equip a farm with stock and implements. The intention, as I understood it, was that it would supply a suitable foundation stock; it would supply the initial bare needs for implements, and the farmer would go on from there. In addition to these amounts, it is well recognized that farm income does not come in monthly, and so provision has been made, for the first year, for monthly payments where necessary to the farmer to maintain him. The single man will receive something like $44 a month and the married man $68, while the married man with children will receive additional allowances for the children. Adding all these benefits together, we have a total of at least $3,000 for one man if he wants to go farming, and I repeat that many farmers in this country, reasonably prosperous, think they do very well by their sons in setting them up in farming if they make a contribution anything like that.
There may be some reason for criticism on the score that the benefits that accrue with respect to a farm costing not more than $4,800 are not adequate. Another clause in the act, which is quite elastic, provides that if a farmer wishes to buy a farm in excess of that amount he is permitted to do so but he must finance the balance himself.
I am coming to the one and only criticism I have-and I would not dream of criticizing such an act without offering what in my opinion is a helpful suggestion. I think that in some parts of the country farms are at such a price that $4,800 would not buy a good up-to-date productive farm.' In that event I think the amount should be increased, but I would correspondingly increase the mortgage

Department of Reconstruction
liability at 34 [DOT] per cent which the veteran assumes. With that one minor amendment,
I think the act would work well, and that is the only complaint I have received from veterans' associations in my riding with respect to the act.
In rising to take part in this debate on the second reading of the bill to provide for the setting up of a department charged with the sole responsibility of post-war reconstruction,
I do so simply to emphasize one problem which I think we shall be facing in the postwar period, and one which I think should be given a No. 1 priority. The general field has been ably covered and I do not intend to spend much time in that regard. While I agree that Canada's post-war prosperity is in part dependent upon the extent to which we are able to assist in achieving world-wide recovery, and while I agree that Canada must assume her full responsibility in that regard, and fully realize that in so far as we do have world-wide recoveiy Canada as a trading nation will participate in the benefits which flow therefrom, yet I feel just as strongly that living conditions in Canada also depend upon the way in which we treat our own local domestic problems. If our national income, whether large or small, is equitably distributed among the different classes of the population, then we shall achieve a proper distribution of goods. I do not think that happened during the depression, but I will not take time now to discuss the causes.
To be permanently prosperous I believe the country must maintain a standard of living on a par with its ability to produce goods. I think that is axiomatic, but there is just one "if," namely, if a country produces goods in excess of its own needs, in order to maintain this high standard of living I am talking about markets must be found for the excess.
As to the production surplus over and above our own consumption needs, which amounts in round figures to one-third of our total production, we should of course exchange that surplus for goods of other countries which we can use. If by foreign trade we are able to do this, we achieve our maximum prosperity. If we cannot do this by foreign trade, I suggest that under the best of management we would only reach two-thirds of our maximum . prosperity. If we do not take the necessary steps to dispose of that unexportable surplus a.nd to prevent the endless distress which follows, such as falling prices and the like, we can get into a lot of trouble. Therefore I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that until world recovery takes place to the point where we shall be able to dispose of the exportable surplus we have three options. We can either
give that exportable surplus away to needy nations; we can stop producing it, or we can store it up at fixed prices hoping to be able to sell it in the future. I do not know of any better illustration of what I am talking about than our exportable surplus of wheat.
The problem I have just outlined is one that should be studied very carefully in this country. On the one hand I do not think that we should accept the defeatist attitude and say that we have to wait until general world recovery comes about; nor on the other hand do I think we should fail to assume our responsibilities in the matter of helping to assist general world recovery. As I sard a moment ago, I am not going to discuss to-day the general problem but there is one concrete matter that I should like to bring to the attention of the government and of the - hon. members of this house. It is a post-war problem which I think will merit a No. 1 priority. We have an acute shortage of, houses in this country. Estimates differ, but reliable sources agree that when this war is over we shall have a shortage of over three hundred thousand houses. It is only right and proper that in time of war, with its consequent shortage of labour and materials, we sho'dd Ty to get along with the housing accommodation we have. We have struggled to do that, Mr. Speaker. By rental controls and the like we have done our best to get by the present emergency without any needless expenditure of either labour or materials on the building of houses. While we have been quite correct in postponing house building to meet the needs of war yet in the long run I suggest it is going to turn out to our advantage, because during the immediate post-war period this postponed consumer demand for houses will have to be met, and it will put thousands of men to work.
At the moment we can reasonably hope that the end of the war is not in the too far distant future, and I think we should immediately complete plans for post-war house building. I should like to urge that pilot or key organizations be set up now, which can be quickly expanded when the war is over, to support, and direct house building schemes. In adopting this plan of postponing the supplying of our housing needs until the war is over we have of necessity caused some real distress. To-day many people are living under almost unbearable housing conditions. To some extent this has been the cause of increasing crime, ill-health and the like. In addition to those who are in actual distress, thousands of families are daily living under the threat that their houses will be Sold over their heads and they will have to move, not knowing where they will go. People cheerfully and willingly
Department oj Reconstruction

sndure that sort of thing during war time. But 1 suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the minute this war is over the Canadian people will demand-they have a right to demand-that their proper housing needs be met.
In addition to the acute housing problem which exists at the present time, when thousands of our service men return they will marry and want homes of their own. In addition to giving the housing problem the rating which I believe it deserves, namely, No. 1 priority, I should like to urge that the government sponsor a campaign for every man to own his own home. I do not know of any better time to start than now, when we have such an acute shortage. I should like to urge that credit facilities be made available for this need on a sound business basis. The advantages of home ownership and the disadvantages of tenant occupancy are so apparent that I do not need to labour the point. In these days we hear many discussions of the relative merits of our capitalistic system and socialism. So far as I am concerned the major complaint that I have in regard to the capitalistic system is that we have too few capitalists. I would urge that every man in this country own his own home; every man should become a capitalist. This proposal is not a dream impossible of fulfilment. It is a scheme which if undertaken as a national programme could be quite easily attained in a very short time. To-day many men have to pay rent for their housing accommodation. Is there any man in this country who would not rather pay the same monthly payments on a house which he will eventually own?
Let me say something as to the down payment. We all know that practically everyone in this country is accumulating savings which I suggest in most instances will be sufficient to take care of the ten per cent down payment at the end of the war. To those who have no! been able to acquire the compulsory saving as a down payment I suggest that the new amendment to the Bank Act will meet their difficulties. The banks are going to enter actively the field of small loans repayable on a monthly basis at a reasonable rate of interest. A man desiring to own his own home would be able to acquire his down payment from, that source.
In the National Housing Act we have a well-tried instrument at hand. We do not need to create anything new to get on with this programme. Do hon. members know that since 1937, under the National Housing Act, we have built something over 25,000 houses? They are practically all owner-occupied; and while the government has participated to the extent of a twenty-five per cent contribution
(Mr. Cleaver.]
toward the cost of those houses, the act was so well thought out and has been so efficiently managed that our losses to date on the
25,000	houses are less than $5,000, or twenty cents per house. I suggest that the present act should be used for this purpose-with some amendments, or streamlined if you like-in order to bring those advantages within the reach of every working man in the country.
My first suggestion is in regard to interest rates. Interest rates should be reduced to 4| per cent, and to 4 per cent if possible. As all hon. members know, money is now available in the Dominion of Canada-that is longterm borrowing-at 3 per cent, or less. Let us take the government's contribution of 25 per cent, and figure it on a 3 per cent basis. Let us allow the loan companies 5 per cent on their 75 per cent loan content, and we have a resulting interest rate of 4| per cent. [DOT]
I suggest if we are to adopt a large building programme the lending institutions of the country may not have sufficient money to finance it on that basis, and that perhaps the government should enter the field on a 50 per cent basis with 3 per cent money. In this event, allowing the loan companies 5 per cent on their 50 per cent content, the interest rate would automatically fall to 4 per cent. With the interest rate at 4J per cent-and the Minister of Finance has announced in advance that that is what is going to happen-the monthly payments for these houses, under which a man actually acquires eventual ownership, are today less than the normal rental for houses of that type. With a possibility of a further one-half per cent reduction, one can see what the effect would be in connection with monthly payments.	[DOT]
Coming to the second recommendation, in connection with the repayment of loans, I know something about these houses built under the National Housing Act. They are well-built. I say without fear of successful contradiction that homes built under the National Housing Act standards have a useful owner-occupancy lifetime of at least forty years. I therefore suggest and urge that the amortization period should be increased from twenty to at least thirty years. That again will assist in bringing down the amounts of monthly payments. The Minister of Finance has already announced that that proposal is under discussion, and that some progress will be made. I would urge as strongly as I can that thirty years should be the minimum, where an owner requires that time to pay for his home.
My next suggested change is a new one. In the mind of each of these home owners is the constant dread, the constant worry hanging

Department oj Reconstruction
over his head that something may happen, possibly through illness or accident, as a result of which the breadwinner would lose his life and the widow would be left with an unbearable mortgage load. If this is to be a nation-wide scheme for every man to own his own home, then I say that in the event of his death the mortgage should be paid off and the widow should be presented with the house free from encumbrances; and that this should be paid out of an insurance fund. I am told that this type of term insurance could be acquired at moderate cost, not exceeding one dollar per home per month.
*My next suggestion deals with restraint in respect of alienation. Very serious thought should be given to this matter. So far as I am concerned, the owner of a house should be placed in the position where he could not, through bad business judgment or in any other way, lose his house. I would have the house in such a position that it will not be subject to execution levies. In addition, I think it might be wise to prevent the owner himself from selling his house, or possibly it would be well in the event of sale to freeze the selling price, or set it apart to be used only for the purchase of another house. That is only my own thought on the subject, but I offer it for what it is worth.
These five suggestions will in my opinion make the act workable and bring it within the reach of every working man in Canada. However we could not possibly succeed in reaching a point where every man would own his own home unless we were to provide for the use of existing houses already built. I suggest that an additional part be added to the housing act to make these second-hand houses, if I may so describe them, available for exactly the same purposes and on quite the same terms. I concede at once that the amortization period should not be so long-that is, it should not exceed the life of the house. In addition, money should be made available by borrowing, repayable in monthly payments, just as under Part I of the aot, to provide for necessary permanent repairs and permanent alterations to bring the existing houses up to modern condition.
If those things are done, and a nation-wide campaign is instituted, it would be almost impossible to estimate the amount of human happiness and human satisfaction which might flow therefrom.
I have commented on the urgency for the need for housing. I have commented, too, on the benefits, peace of mind and human happiness which would flow from such a plan. I have one other reason why in my opinion
housing should receive priority in connection with post-war reconstruction, and it is this: The labour content of every medium sized house is at least eighty per cent. Some members may question that percentage, but when I refer to labour content I am not referring only to the labour expended in the building of the house. I include the indirect labour- the labour content that goes into the manufacture of frames, doors, lumber, flooring, plaster, hardware, plumbing, and everything else used in construction. If one computes all that in the labour content he will reach at least eighty per cent labour content in a medium sized home. I do not know of any type of construction in which the labour content is as great. For that reason therefore I say that is one of the post-war schemes we should first adopt.
There is another feature in connection with labour content, and it is this: I do not know of any construction work in which the labour content would be so diversified, and spread out over the entire country. One might say it would be spread throughout all branches of industry. Benefits would accrue to all parts of the country.
For all these reasons I urge as strongly as I can that the present is not one day too soon to make plans and to complete the organization for the financing and the supplying of materials for the new houses we so urgently need.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not apologize for taking part in this debate in connection with the establishment of a Department of Reconstruction. I agree entirely with the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), who has said that this matter is next in importance to that of winning the war or prosecuting the war. Had I not said anything I am afraid I would have been apologizing to myself for some considerable time. I suppose when I finish my speech I will still be apologizing to myself because of having fallen far short of what I would have liked to say 'in the short time at my disposal and with my limited ability.
I have been interested in this matter from almost the start of the war. So far as I know the first committee on rehabilitation set up in Canada was one set up in British Columbia by the British Columbia branch of the Canadian Manufacturers' association. I happened to be chairman of that branch at the time. I believe that committee is still functioning and considering plans for rehabilitation and reconstruction. I remember one statement that I made at the annual meeting. I impressed upon all the manufacturers of
Department oj Reconstruction

British Columbia the necessity of watching their plants very closely in order that they should not run down. I emphasized the fact that obsolescence was a detriment not only *o the particular plant but to the province as a whole.
I took another step at that time in an effort to enlarge the knowledge of this subject, both in the province and throughout Canada, but this was a somewhat disappointing experience. I offered an award for the best essay on postwar rehabilitation to be written by any undergraduate in Canada. This offer was made directly to the James committee when it was first formed, and it was also passed along to the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) who received it very warmly. However, the universities did not seem to rise to the occasion and give this suggestion the leadership which I thought it should have received. Instead of announcing this award to their students at the close of the year, they announced it when the college term opened, and the result was that only a few participated because they had only some three or four weeks to prepare their essays.
I would be quite prepared to continue this offer for the duration of the war. I think if it had been done we would have had a young people who were more enlightened on this subject. There are many young people reaching the time of life when they might make an active study of these matters, but they have not had the opportunity. If they are prepared to make full use of my offer I am prepared to renew it at this time.
I regretted that the statement was made in the house that this department was being set up to fill a temporary need only. I think that is a mistake. It should be a department for the development of Canada not only in the transition period from war to peace but for the many years to come. The department should be available for as long as it is necessary, and I am sure that that will be for the lifetime of Canada. There is so much in this country that is yet untouched. There are tremendous possibilities for development, and I cannot see anything better than to have an all-time department. This should not be a department with just a minister, a deputy minister and a few assistants; it should be a department with a minister, a deputy minister and a staff sufficiently large that its members could be selected from all parts of Canada, thus bringing together the necessary knowledge for this particular sphere of development.
The other day we heard a splendid speech by the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene). He told us a little-no one could

tell us all-of that great northland of which we know so little. There are over a million square miles filled with every kind of natural resource, such as minerals, forests, fisheries and oil. I am sure it will take some time fully to develop this particular district.
Speaking a few days ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) mentioned another possible field of development. He referred to the creating of Ottawa as a federal district, and the possibilities of beautifying the nation's capital. He told us how it was hoped to make the other bank of the Ottawa river in Hull a thing of beauty. There should not only be a physical development of Canada; we should have cultural development as well. There are many cities besides Ottawa where similar projects could be carried out. I am one who believes that it is not a waste of money to develop cultural things. Would anyone say that money has been wasted in the construction of this grand building we are in at the present time? We could actually do with much less in the way of a building. We could talk just as much, although there might be a greater fire risk. But will anyone say that it has been a waste of money? Will anyone say that what was done on Elgin street a few years ago was a waste of money? I definitely say that it was not. We could take every city in Canada and try to make it a city beautiful as well as a city useful.
Any schoolboy will tell you that we must develop our industries to their maximum. These things are so obvious that they scarcely need mention. But the others are things which we have been overlooking. It is a change of mind that we want towards our development. Take, for instance, the city of Winnipeg, or Saskatoon, Regina, Edmonton, Vancouver; or take my own city, the city of Victoria. I do not think there is a more beautiful spot in Canada than Victoria, and regardless of what anyone else says, it is the playground and will remain the playground of Canada so far as climate is concerned. The nation could spend in the city of Victoria many millions of dollars which would be of tremendous advantage not only to the people of the city of Victoria but to the rest of Canada who would be glad to get away from the winters you have in the east. People are coming into the city of Victoria from all directions, both summer and winter. It is the only place where you can have really warm salt water bathing practically the year round. By the expenditure of a few hundred thousand dollars you could make it not only a national but an international playground to the great advantage of us all. I had no intention of

Department oj Reconstruction
bringing forward the claims of my own city for development. I use it just as an illustration of the possibilities that we have in Canada for just such projects.

speechtext:
I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that I am anxious to see these developments take place; I emphasize this because there is not time to deal with the others, and I want if possible to get this point across.
I believe that we have to have full employment. I do not believe you can have half of your people employed and the other half unemployed. Someone has said that no man is free unless all are free, and I do not think we can be busy to the best advantage unless we are all busy. I think we could all be busy in ihe future.
In the programme which should be undertaken the matter of tempo enters. Some say that the tempo should be increased just as soon as the boys come home from overseas.
inft-259
Personally I do not think so. I believe that there will be sufficient work, more than sufficient work, for the first two or three and possibly four years after the war is over. It will be in the subsequent period that we may have to move in and find work for people to do; but this nation I think will do these things I have mentioned because they are in the end self-supporting. I want to emphasize that.
I do not think you should bring the boys home from overseas and put them to work and at the same time leave the boys that are at home without work to do, because when one man is idle, somebody else is not fully employed. Only when all are employed can all be fully employed.
I am going to make four suggestions, and then I shall conclude.
First I think the name ''Reconstruction" is a misnomer. It has come out of its association with rehabilitation. It is national construction, national planning on a long and broad scale which in my opinion is required. Rehabilitation is an entirely different matter.
I do not say that they are separable, because you cannot have rehabilitation without reconstruction. But title reconstruction would mean that this country has been, partly destroyed or that we intend to destroy it and rebuild it. There is nothing of the kind. We are to build on what we have. It is a gradual development on the basis of our imagination, and, I hope, of our courage, because I know that our ability to do it is there. I suggest that the name of this department be changed.
I suggest, too, that it be made a permanent department. I suggest that it have a large personnel, not a small one; that that large personnel be selected from all parts of Canada, and that in their planning they look towards developing not only the ribbon that runs across Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific, but Canada as a whole.
I suggest also that the minister, whoever he may be, be appointed now. I do not think it is too early. The formation of this branch of government is very timely, and the minis

ter should be appointed now for this reason. He would be able to sit in on and give a lead to the banking and commerce committee, because finance is going to come into the programme of reconstruction, and his advice and assistance in planning for the reorganization, if that is to take place, should be of some assistance both to him and to us.
I suggest that this department be not just another department of government, but that it be "the" department of government, because upon it depends the full work of our people; on the full work of our people depends our

Department oj Reconstruction

national income, and on our national income depends whether or not we can carry on with our social legislation. This department is the heart and the backbone of Canada itself in action.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, most allied nations have been laying plans during the past three or four years for post-war planning and rehabilitation; but I say to you as emphatically as I can, in view of statements which are being made outside the House of Commons, that no country among the allied nations is so far ahead in plans for rehabilitation as is Canada under the present government. That statement cannot be successfully refuted. I am sorry that the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation is not in his seat this afternoon, because I intended at this time to deal with one or two statements he has made; however I will defer until later most of the things I have in mind. I think it is most unfair for an hon. member, especially one who is the leader of a party, to make statements throughout the country which, I say, are not true. For instance, he is quoted as having said a short time ago that two million jobs would have to be found for service men returning to civilian life in Canada after the war, and that not a single plan has been devised by the dominion government to meet that situation. In that utterance there are two gross misstatements of fact. The first one is that two million jobs will be needed for service men. There are not over eight hundred thousand men and women in the armed forces of Canada, and to assert publicly that two million jobs will be required for them is a kind of mathematics which is beyond me. I rather thought that people in the country from which I come knew something about mathematics and education.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Some statements have been made during this debate, either in the speeches or in cross-fire conversations across the floor of the house, particularly by members of the C.C.F., regarding the years of depression, 1930 to 1939. Speakers of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group have gibed at both the Conservative and the Liberal parties with reference to the great amount of unemployment during those years. I have been frank to admit wherever I have gone that there was a great deal of unemployment at that time, but I do not understand the reasoning of those who remind us of it, or why Canada in particular should be singled out and our form of democratic government denounced because we were not able to solve the problem during those years. No country in the world, I care not what form of government it had, solved the problem. Oh, yes; someone is going to say that all were working fully in Russia, that they were fully occupied in Germany and Italy and Japan. But if all those countries had their people at work, it was simply because they were getting ready for war. We are not a warlike country. The facts are that no country in the world solved the

Department oj Reconstruction
problem of unemployment during those years- neither Russia nor Germany, Italy nor Japan. Yet members of the C.C.F. go up and down the country saying that we must have a new form of democratic government, that the old parties have failed, because from 1930 to 1939 they did not solve unemployment.
The thought has just entered my mind, and it is something I have long wanted to say in this house, that I have been astonished at the attitude of a number of those who, have come to Canada from other lands and who, had they stayed in the lands they came from, would probably not have owned very much; yet with all the possible things that God could give them in this great land, they have gone around denouncing the government of Canada. I remind the house, and it seems to me a strange and significant fact, that during the years of depression, and when we were hearing so much of the progress of Russia, although
60,000	persons made application to the Canadian government to be taken back to Great Britain, no applications so far as I can learn were made by any who came from the countries of continental Europe to be returned to the country of their origin or birth.
I say, Mr. Speaker, let us have some pride in our land. When one looks over the membership of this house and recalls that some thirty-one hon. members were born outside this country and came to it from nine different countries, it seems reasonable to ask whether there is any other land which has provided the same opportunities as this great country has provided to those who have come here from abroad. One quality in the Russian people which we might well emulate is their great love of country.
While I am not suggesting that this government should adopt the policies of militarily-minded states, it is my opinion that following the conclusion of this war we shall not allow ourselves for many, many years to revert to the condition of unpreparedness in which we found ourselves prior to 1939.
One thing we all admire about Prime Minister Churchill is the great frankness of his statements. It is a splendid thing to be frank. When he was speaking in the British House of Commons on post-war rehabilitation someone reminded him that after the last war British shipowners had bought German merchant ships at a cost of little or nothing. He replied that that was perfectly true, but, he said, "We won't make that mistake again, though I expect," he said, "being human, we shall make other mistakes." I recall that because we too admit frankly, at least I do, that we did make a mistake in 1930 to 1939. But we are not going to repeat
that mistake; and when anyone goes through this country endeavouring t'o persuade the people that a new heaven or a new earth will come about if only some new type of democratic government is given an opportunity, I warn the public to be very careful before they take such statements too literally.
It is only of late that members of the C.C.F. party have admitted that trade may be at all a significant factor. Like most parties, they are keeping their ear to the ground too and moving along as they think the people want them to, so that they do not differ from any of the older parties in that political regard. That, after all, is democracy. I do not know what the future will bring forth, but if past history has been any guide to us at all it shows us this. To me at least it has proved that the nations that have gone out to trade, and to trade freely, have been the nations which have given most of this world's goods to their people, while the nations who have lived unto or within themselves have been the nations which have given the least of this world's goods to their people. That has been the history of mankind from the days of Adam to the present time, and it is my opinion that the same thing will hold good for many years to come. We must therefore pay greater attention to international trade.
This country is adapted to produce great quantities of grain, lumber, fish and agricultural products which could never be consumed at home unless we trebled our population, even though we were provided with twice the amount of food we consume at the present time. I find that the Liberal party is in pretty good company, because at the international labour conference held in Philadelphia in May last the following statement was made with regard to trade, enunciating the fact that we must take note of what is taking place in other lands:
The war against want requires to be carried on with unrelenting vigour within each nation, and by continuous and concerted international effort in which the representatives of workers and employers, enjoying equal status with those of governments, join with them in free discussions and democratic decision with a view to the promotion of the common welfare.
And this is what I ask you to note particularly. This is an outstanding resolution:
Poverty anywhere constitutes a danger to prosperity everywhere.
That is the point of view held by those of the Liberal party who are looking to the furtherance of trade, believing that we cannot remain in our shell or live unto ourselves and hope to prosper. Isolation, sir, is as dead to-day
Department of Reconstruction

as the great wall of China. When one realizes that it takes only about sixty hours to travel completely round the globe, one realizes how close countries are to Qne another and that we must pay greater attention to the prosperity and well-being of other countries as well as the prosperity and well-being of our own. When we think of the brotherhood of man, we must realize that this brotherhood was not intended to be confined within the borders of any one country.
In British Columbia for many years, emanating from those belonging to the C.C.F. and emanating as well from members of the C.C.F. party in this house, there have come public utterances upholding the Dominion of New Zealand. The other day an hon. member pointed out, in answer to an interruption, that the general picture of welfare in this country was ahead of that of New Zealand. I have gone into this matter a little, and these are some of the things I find. Take the debt charges in New Zealand, for instance-and I have the debt charge translated into dollars so as to make it comparable with that of our own country. The public debt charge of this country is on an average $6S0 per head, while in New Zealand it is $1,010. Take interest charges. We have heard a great deal about interest charges and debt-free money, but there again we are still ahead of New Zealand. Interest charges in Canada amount to 2-90 per cent- and I understand even that has been reduced -whereas in New Zealand the interest charges are 3-42 per cent. We have heard a great deal about the load of debt on the Canadian people. Well, the load of interest debt in Canada works out at something like $14.65 per head, whereas in New Zealand the load of debt is $28.75. I have given the interest charges they are paying on loans, and I have given the public debt. Now, coming to taxation, this may interest hon. members. I have not time to go into it fully, but I shall be pleased on another occasion to elaborate on these matters individually. The single man in New Zealand earning $700 pays something like $53. In Canada it works out at $26, with $13 refundable. The married man with two children earning $1,500 per annum pays in Canada $49.50, with $24 refundable. In New Zealand he pays $154. This information I have obtained from the New Zealand Fear Book.

You are insulting a sister

speechtext:
I resent that. I am not insulting anyone. I am putting these facts before the house only for one purpose. It has been held up to the people of this country by the C.C.F. that if we adopted a government similar to that in New Zealand all the good things people hope for would be bestowed on the Canadian people. I am not bringing this forward for any other purpose than to answer my hon. friend. I do not wish to introduce division between sister dominions, but it is said so often by members of the C.C.F., both in British Columbia and here, that I am impelled to correct their statements and keep the record right and true. When it comes to taxation, it would appear that they soak the workers there. We in Canada place the burden of taxation where we believe it can best be borne. For in the matter of income tax they pay more in New Zealand until the sum of $10,000 per annum is reached, and thereafter it gets less, whereas in Canada it increases very greatly indeed. I could quote bond interest too, which is less in Canada. In regard to New Zealand's financial position I doubt, Mr. Speaker, had it not been for the help of Great Britain during the war, whether she would have been in as good a financial position to-day as her books would seem to indicate.
With regard to Canada and rehabilitation, may I say without fear of successful contradiction that the provision we have made for our service men is not bettered or equalled by any other country of the allied nations. There is only one thing that I believe New Zealand has done a little better than we, and that is with regard to the matter of clothing allowance. I hope that will be adjusted in Canada before very long. In the matter of treatment, pensions and hospitalization for service men, I know of no country which is doing more than we are. In saying that I do iaot want to leave the impression that we have finished or reached the ultimate in the treatment of our service men and women. I am

Department oj Reconstruction
merely stating the fact. If anyone has any statement to make to the contrary I shall be glad to hear it.
British Columbia is taking quite a part in the work of rehabilitation. The government of that province set up a committee composed of representatives of all parties in the assembly. The report of that committee emphasized the matter of finance. The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruiekshank) in his speech this afternoon touched on the subject of municipal finances. While I realize that no definite projects can be outlined at the moment, the general plans are, however, outlined, and the government of the day should as soon as possible let the cities and municipalities know what their position will be in regard to loans. If the municipalities could obtain loans at cost, say, three-quarters of one per cent, I feel sure that every city and municipality would immediately set to work to outline post-war works. Remember, Mr. Speaker, that a great deal of the burden of rehabilitation will fall on these cities and municipalities, because when a man is seeking relief, and sometimes when he is seeking employment, the first place to which he goes is the municipal council. In every recommendation presented on behalf of the government of British Columbia that one point was brought out.
I am not going to weary the house because this document is too voluminous for me to place on Hansard, but I wish to read one of the recommendations that was put before the dominion government. It is as follows:
No information seems to be available as to what procedure will be followed by the dominion government in allocating proportions of cost under any of the rehabilitation programmes where they operate to the benefit of municipalities. Naturally a programme involving one and a half million dollars is entirely beyond the capacity of most cities.
Then further:
Your committee appeared before the provincial government rehabilitation committee early this year-
That was 1943.
-presented their report, and entered into a discussion regarding some of the proposals, especially regarding the method of financing post-war schemes. We feel that until the question of finances has been settled, the whole work of all post-war committees has been futile. The provincial committee themselves have not a solution, as they in turn await the decision of the federal government on this point.
Therefore I urge upon the Prime Minister and the government the necessity of arriving at a decision as soon as practicable, and so that the municipalities, cities and provincial governments be informed as to what help they
may expect from the dominion government and what rates of interest will be charged for loans.
I would make one other proposal to the Prime Minister and to the government. Before the programme of rehabilitation starts, steps should be taken with regard to the debts owing the dominion government by provincial governments. I was looking over this matter before I came down to the chamber this afternoon, and I was surprised to find that according to the last auditor general's report the provincial governments owed the dominion government something like $313,309,016-and by the way, Saskatchewan did very well in that respect because that province was lent a considerable sum of money, according to the record; they owe the government $79,828,017. As one looks over the staggering amounts one realizes that that is one of the things that should be taken up at either the forthcoming dominion-provincial conference or as soon as possible thereafter, to see if some means can be devised for clearing up those debts which hang like a cloud over the provincial governments. The provincial governments in turn have lent large sums of money to municipalities, and those debts also hang like a cloud over the municipalities.
In his speech of yesterday afternoon the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) made some reference to the fisheries. I am not going extensively into the matter of fisheries this afternoon, but in looking through the recommendations and statements made by the government I notice that fisheries have been mentioned as one form of rehabilitation. May I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that in so far as British Columbia is concerned I doubt whether we can take many more men into the fishing industries. We may be able to take more men, women and youths into the canning factories, but I doubt whether we can place or take care of any more men as fishermen. I say that for this reason: the quantity of fish in our waters is, after all, limited, and the more men put into the industry the smaller the return will be for the individual fisherman. However, there is one branch of the fishing industry into which we could place more men. I refer to the halibut fisheries. Under the provisions of the international halibut treaty the yearly allotment of the United States and Canada is something like fifty million pounds. We have never been able to take more than one-third of our share. The United States fishermen have been able to take the larger part, up to three-quarters of the amount allotted. They can do that because they have larger and better fishing vessels which can go
Department oj Reconstruction

farther afield. They are better fitted to withstand the rough seas one or two hundred miles off our shore. Canada is bearing fifty per cent of the cost of the halibut fishery commission. Is there any reason why our fishermen should not be encouraged to take their fifty per cent of the allotment?
Since 1939 some ninety large fishing vessels have been taken from the fishing industry in British Columbia for military purposes. These boats, or better ones, should be put back for the specific purpose of fishing for halibut. Everything that it is possible to do should be done to enable our fishermen to compete with United States fishermen on the halibut banks. When the Japanese were taken out of British Columbia and the fishing licences were curtailed in 1941, it was stated that the fishing industry would suffer. It may interest the house to hear actual figures, and to know what the results have been since the Japanese left the fishing industry.
There were 1,337 Japanese fishing vessels taken over from the Japanese, and sold, the money being held to the credit of the individuals concerned. In 1941 there was a total of 13,602 fishing licences in all issued in British Columbia. Of that number the Japanese held 2,080, or 15-4 per cent. In 1942-43 the number of fishing licences increased until, at the last issue, they amounted to 15,379, an increase of 1,777. The actual picture is that 3,857 more fishermen have entered into the fishing industry since the Japanese left British Columbia. I would ask this very practical question of the C.C.F. In their rehabilitation programme will they allow the Japanese to return to the fishing industry of British Columbia? I would like to have that luestion answered. My stand is that they should not come back. The fishermen of British Columbia, however, should be told. They should be told whether if the C.C.F. were elected to power the Japanese would be allowed to come back into the fishing industry, because at the present time, with 15,379 licences issued, there is not a decent living for many more.

speechtext: That is the body which should make a decision, because it is a British Columbia matter.

speechtext:
The issuing of licences is not a British Columbia matter. It is not the provincial government which will make the decision; it is the people of British Columbia who will make it when the proper time comes. However, I want a statement in that connection, because I do not want the people to be misled. When they vote they should know what they are voting for.
I see my time is going on, and I shall proceed with my closing observations. In connection with rehabilitation I would say that first consideration must be given our fighting men; for without their sacrifice no rehabilitation or social security would be possible for us. While plans are being laid now to rehabilitate the men and women in our active forces after the war, and likewise to provide employment and other social measures for our citizens generally, much more thought will have to be given to world conditions than has been given to them by our people. Social security cannot be assured us unless we can be assured of a reasonable and lasting peace following the end of this war; and there can be no national security in a policy of isolation. One of the great problems facing the allies now, aside from the w'inning of the war, is how we can prevent another blood bath in the future; for the winning of the war may not bring peace.
For the past few years statements have been made throughout Canada about the danger of winning the war and losing the peace. While what is meant by losing the peace is open to many interpretations, to my mind one danger facing us is that owing to careless thinking on our part, or to not thinking at all, we may lose what freedom there is left. To many people, thinking is hard work. History can show many examples of peoples who have lost their liberty because they were too lazy to think out for themselves the problems that all free peoples must solve if they are to continue free. To my mind dangerous fires are being lighted in the minds of the people these days, fires w'hich may flare up and consume us before we fully realize what it is all about.
Underneath a lot of the loose talk uttered to-day the real issue is not readily seen. That real issue is not so much economic as it is philosophic. The real issue is whether we

Department oj Reconstruction
should trust to the state supreme power over our lives. Never let us forget that our fathers found out long ago that complete power over our lives could not be trusted to anyone, no matter how wise or how virtuous a king or even a government might be. Men preferred to live their own lives; and so there was devised a society with power of its own to resist the government. If ever the state obtains complete mastery of our lives, freedom will be gone for ever. Once a single power, whether the state, the capitalist, the labour unions or any other group, undertakes to run our lives according to a certain plan and to guarantee by that plan to produce certain results, then it can brook no interference; for if the plan fails the rulers lose either their jobs or their lives.
It must not be inferred from what I say in this regard that I am advocating that we must not have new rules to prevent greed and the exploitation of the great masses of our people. New rules will have to be provided-yes, and enforced-so as to ensure a fuller and better life for all our citizens. In doing so, however, let us be very careful that we do not throw away for a mess of pottage the most cherished jewel of all, namely our individual freedom. The right to live one's own life, the right of free speech, the right to worship God in our own way-all these are a heritage which to me is priceless, and can never be compensated for by material things alone. It is as true to-day as when spoken by Christ, when he said, "Man shall not live by bread alone."

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to say a few words to-day in the debate on this bill, because I believe it brings into focus the culmination of a long series of events since the turn of the century. This happens to be the first time any government in Canada has assumed the responsibility of setting up a department of economic direction.
The powers in the bill, which are to be vested in the minister and which are being delegated by parliament to the governor in council, vest in the new ministry a power over the economic well-being of individuals in Canada which, in itself, would have caused a revolution only a few years ago. Just what the exercise of those powers may be will be for history to disclose. But I think the acceptance of the provision for the wide powers extended to the ministry indicates that the government is well conversant not only with the seriousness of the problems which lie ahead, but also with the enormous difficulties which will attend their solution.
I for one hold the firm conviction that Canada is well provided to meet with success the post-war period, notwithstanding my belief
that the difficulties will be just as great anc just as costly as have been the problems ol sustaining the economy of the nation through this period of war. There is no chart to guide us now as there was no chart to guide us when we embarked on the war in 1939.
I think some facts stand out, and here are what I consider the general broad conceptions of the main problem. Gainful employment will have to be provided for some five million Canadians, two million of whom are now engaged in the fighting services and in war industry. We have a public debt already of $14 billion, and upon any reasonable basis of estimation this will be rising for some time to a figure much larger than that. Already we have $11 billion of national federal debt, $2 billion of provincial debt and $1 billion of municipal debt.
Do not make any mistake about the condition of our provinces and municipalities. Representatives of both have appeared before the reconstruction committee. The Hon. Mr. Garson, Premier of Manitoba, pointed out in great detail that that province will have revenues wholly inadequate to provide for a greatly expanded programme of expenditure. I am confident that while every province has gleaned something from deferred maintenance during the war and from war revenues, there is not one which under its existing revenue powers has the financial resources to hope to make up in the post-war period the deferred maintenance that has accumulated during the war years.
Those who are interested in Mr. Garson's views will find them in the evidence of the reconstruction and reestablishment committee, No. 19, page 486, June 2, 1942. On November 27, 1943, representatives of the mayors' federation of Canada appeared before the committee and stated:
The financial resources of the municipalities are wholly inadequate for any large scale postwar public works programme such as probably will be required.
That was not so after the last war. At the close of the last war the provincial and municipal governments embarked, not only upon a programme of making up deferred maintenance but upon a progressive programme of general expansion. On the other hand, the dominion government curtailed expenditures and moved toward a programme of balanced budgets with the objective of reducing the national debt.
Many people ask, and with some justification, "Are we going to move from this war into a period of illusionary prosperity and then collapse into a condition of hopeless inactivity?" There was never anything wrong with the wealth of Canada from 1930 to 1939, but
Department of Reconstruction

there was something wrong with the machinery that maintained in circulation the economic power of the collective society of the people of Canada. We were told after the last war, "You have spent your money; the war has caused this debt; you have to tighten your belt and meet your obligations." No one can find much fault with that kind of honest theorizing.
Unfortunately, however, when the government stopped spending the country lost the power to expand, and all of a sudden the complete collapse of the economic structure took place. I should like to draw to the attention of the government and the minister some facts which are indicative that the financing of this war has followed closely the pattern of the financing of the last war. ' There are some details which vary greatly, but let me direct attention to the fact that in 1941 our total bank deposits were $1,052 million, while in 1918 they were $1,942 million. We increased our bank deposits by SS42 million.
What have we done in this war? In 1938 our bank deposits were $2,498 million, and in April, 1943, they had risen to $5,297 million. Do not make any mistake about what that means. It means that the debt claim currency of this country, which was the cause of the trouble after the last war, has shown a proportionately larger increase during this war than it did in the last. That is not national currency circulating as a servant of the people; that is not currency issued in terms of public need; that is debt claim currency which is not spent into circulation as an operating medium of exchange but lent into circulation as a debt claim upon the nation to provide a monopoly. Make no mistake about what that means. If that is not changed, this system of frustrating every effort of progress, breaking down every power to move forward, all the plans, yes, all the sacrifices of this war will have been in vain.
Let me refer to another similarity. We have gone through this before and we are going through it again. Do not think for one moment that we on this continent will be given any special dispensation. What will permit us to escape the consequences which have befallen the people of Europe if we make the mistakes the people of Europe have made? In 1914 our public debt load was $335 million. By 1918 it had risen to $1,191 million, an increase of $S66 million. But let me give the increase in the debt load since 1939. In 1939 we owed a debt of $4,693,000,000. On December 31, 1943, it had increased to $11,300,000,000. The increase in the federal debt in 1918 was $866,000,000, and to-day it is already $6,609,-

000,000. That debt must be serviced. Our interest charges have risen, although the rate has beeen cut, from $169,000,000 to- $304,000,000. Our interest charges at the close of the last war were less than a hundred million dollars, and yet we heard those responsible for the government of Canadian cities, those responsible for the government of our provinces and those responsible for our federal government declaring throughout the whole of the period from 1920 to 1929 that the crippling power, the all-evading restricting force upon Canadian democracy in all its services to the people lay in the fact that there were fixed charges that could not be reduced; it lay in the fact that the debt load had increased to the point where nothing could be done without deficit budgeting, which is against sound, practical, financial economy.
What is the solution of that problem today, for it is not going to solve itself, and the men of to-morrow in our cities, in our provincial governments and in this parliament cannot escape finding a solution of this problem. I have listened to a great many ministers of finance. But I have never heard one minister of finance who approved deficit financing. I have never heard a responsible public man declare that a nation or a province or a city or an individual could go on and maintain its or his economic security by pyramiding an ever-increasing load of interest-bearing debt. There is plenty of evidence to prove that that debt load is a menace to-day.
You, see, Mr. Speaker, it is all very well to say to the people: Your debts must be paid. The moment you start regimenting your people or imposing upon them a burden of taxation, you face one of two things. You face open revolt and repudiation of the government, and at the same time you face the line of diminishing returns. We are already at that point in Canada.
I support heartily what I thought was a splendid presentation of the situation by the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) the other evening. But men say: How can you reduce taxation and increase public services? How can you call upon the government to cut down its levy of taxes on the people and to extend its expending power to providte services and improvements which the people are demanding? And we come to that easy phrase, You cannot get something for nothing. That on the face of it seems to be reasonable. But certainly under the existing system of issuing the medium of exchange, not in terms of public need, but in terms of private gain, through a toll-gate of interest imposed by

Department of Reconstruction
private monopoly, you cannot escape the disaster of overwhelming and unpayable debt.
What is there in the way of solution? There was a time when men believed that the medium of exchange available to the people deipended on the amount of money metal they could' dig out of the ground. When the cycle of trade depression came around, unless you could discover a gold mine in California or Australia or perhaps the Cariboo, poverty would have to remain. As late as 1930 I heard the then- Prime Minister, of this country declare that gold is an asset necessary to our credit and that without our gold reserves our money would be valueless.
What has happened to that theory? It has gone, and gold has not lost its value. Gold plays a great part, as well as silver, in our international world to-day, and it probably will continue to play that part. But make no mistake about it, we have been released forever from the restricting powers of gold upon the volume of our internal currency, and to-day The Bank of Canada dollar, printed with a printing press upon a piece of paper, has behind it the integrity of the government, the resources of the entire nation and the intelligence of the Canadian people.
We have a means of creating a medium of exchange and putting it into circulation without accumulating an ever-increasing burden of debt. I just want to go back a little while, because what I am preaching is not new. I came to Ottawa many years ago and I laid before the banking and commerce committee of 1934 these proposals:
The successful operation of the New Deal for humanity proposed by the Liberal party necessitates the establishment of the administrative foundations which I outlined to the banking and commerce committee on May 1, 1934, namely:
(1)	A national banking system controlling the issue of all currency and monetization and issue of credit transferable by cheque.
(2)	A department of taxation empowered to prevent excessive accumulation of currency and credit in issue;
(3)	A department of economy for the regulation and control of all internal trade, commerce and credit;
(4)	A department of foreign trade for the development, control and regulation of international trade, commerce, currency and credit.
This plan does not involve the socialization of private finance or the wiping out of the legitimate business of the merchant banker. It can and should be confined to the national administration of currency and public credit devoted to the financing of all public enterprise and the maintenance of an adequate stream of consumers' buying power. Under this plan the national government, working in cooperation with the provincial and municipal authorities throughout the dominion can eliminate the
disastrous costs which the private money system now imposes upon the financing of all public enterprise. We can eliminate unemployment, reestablish a rising standard of living, and advance our internal and external trade. Education may continue to iron out the social and economic inequalities which unfortunately persist. Steps to secure a greater measure of equity in the distribution of wealth may be undertaken with greater hope of success. Government will be able to function more effectively in maintaining a fairer balance between the city, agricultural and industrial communities. We do not assume that the Dominion of Canada can maintain economic independence, but we do say that under this plan the government of the dominion will be able to maintain, in cooperation with those nations who are willing and anxious to trade with us, a measure of economic security that has never been enjoyed in the past.
How much of that plan has been put in effect since 1934? All of it in some degree. The only thing lacking to give the government of Canada to-day power which every democratic government should have is the power to issue currency through its own national institution as the spending power of government.
I asserted at that time that we could not go on indifferent at the head of national government under our constitution to the financial needs and taxation powers and responsibilities of provincial and municipal governments. We found ourselves in those years in the junior branches of government hopelessly without the means of financing undertakings which would have eliminated much of the unemployment in our cities. School-teachers went unpaid. May I say that there is a great group of people throughout our national economy to-day who are underpaid, who are not receiving adequate compensation for the increase in the cost of living, or for the positions which they hold in our social and economic life, or for the services they render to the community at large.
If we are to have a peaceful period of secure progress after the war we have to meet some other problems. After the last war the number of airmen returning was comparatively small as compared with the numbers that will return in the uniform of the Royal Canadian Air Force after this war. The training they have secured and the record they have written in the skies entitle them, yes, entitle them all, to a place in the social order and economic life which will be worthy of the place they now hold. They will rightly demand a place in a nation enjoying a high state of progressive prosperity and they will not be satisfied with anything less. The men and women who will return in the uniform
Department oj Reconstruction

of Canada's navy are highly trained. They nave held an important place. Do you think they are going to be willing to return to be mere hewers of wood and drawers of water? Are they to return to a life in which they may be told to-day that they can have a job and to-morrow that it is not available? So it is with the men and women of our army. They are trained to be leaders in the great forces of mechanized power. Do you think the problem of reestablishing the demobilized forces will be in any respect similar to what it was after the last war? Go through any of your modern factories; look at the people engaged there. The surroundings, the work they are doing, the wages they are receiving, are industrial conditions of the highest standards. Do you think for a moment that they will return to a standard of living such as obtained in Canada from 1930 to 1939? They will not do so. They will not be satisfied to accept it.
How then can this problem be faced? It certainly cannot be faced under the present debt claim system. It cannot be faced under a system of taxation which has already passed the line of diminishing returns and is destroying private enterprise-
