speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King for the second reading of bill No. 82, to establish a Department of Reconstruction.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no desire to detain the house any longer than is necessary for me to make

a few remarks on this bill to set up a Department of Reconstruction. At the outset may I say that I do not believe I have ever before experienced such a tense house as I experienced this afternoon, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) gave his official statement respecting some of our men who were among those who had been shot in Germany as they attempted to escape. Every heart here seemed to be hushed as we thought of it. I may say, too, that I think all hon. members agree with the Prime Minister when he says that such action should not be allowed to go by without punishment eventually- being meted out to those who are responsible. I trust, too, that that punishment will be a penalty to fit the crime.
Some of us have boys in this war; some of us have lost sons in this war; some of us have sons who are prisoners of war, while others have sons who are facing the enemy on the seas, on the battle field and in the skies. Those brave lads who were shot gave up their lives for their country, and I trust that their sacrifice shall not have been in vain.
If the present administration are sincere in setting up this new Department of Reconstruction-and at the present time I have no reason to believe they are otherwise-and if they put their hands to the task and really attempt to bring about a new order in Canada which will give all men their security, and at the same time retain for all men their individual freedom, they will then have done something worthy of the sacrifices made by those young men.
The term "reconstruction" is Something of a misnomer in Canada, because it appears to me that one cannot reconstruct something that is not broken down. So far as Canada is concerned-and the Prime Minister recognized'this in his speech on the bill the other day-we have suffered no bombings. Our entire country is still intact. Our industries have already been built up. It will be a matter of transferring Canada from a war-time industrial nation to a peace-time nation. So far as reconstruction is concerned, I must say that I do not see what there is to reconstruct.	_
I believe, however, there is a great job we need to do. When I think of reconstruction I am wondering if the Prime Minister and his government are not a little bit behind the times. I can recall when as early as 1935 a certain well-honoured gentleman arose in this country and, recognizing that some reconstruction hadi to be done in those days of depression, brought into existence what was known as a reconstruction party. I believe that was the time when we had need to recognize that something was wrong in Canada. That was the

Department of Reconstruction
time when1 this government, the one now in office, should have set its hand to the task of making Canada what it ought to have been.
I know a good deal of reference has been made in this debate to the past. Hon. members, particularly those on the government side, have said, "Oh, well, that is all in the past; we do not want to know about that. We want to know about the future." But I am at a loss to know, and particularly as I analysed the speech of the Prime Minister, what there is he hopes to get in the future that he could not have had in the past. There must be some reason for reconstruction.
The strange thing about it is-and I suppose it is quite explainable-that there have come from all quarters of the country, and I suppose from other countries which have found themselves in similar circumstances, the recognition of a need for reconstruction. We have boards of trade; we have chambers of commerce; we have industrialists; we have committees of the House of Commons and of the government. Why are there all these demands for reconstruction!? I think I can say they have their background in the experience of the past.
While I am talking about the. many plans offered for reconstruction, may I, in passing, call the government's attention to a little book I hold in my hand, a book of only seventy-three pages, entitled, "A Report on Post-War Reconstruction Policies," and issued by the post-war policy committee of the Vancouver board of trade. I do not know if the government's attention has been brought to this book, but I would say that I have read it diligently and I declare that of all the voluminous reports I have read with respect to reconstruction I have never discovered anything containing such valuable information as does this small book. It was not issued by the Social Credit government of Alberta. It -was not issued by the Social Credit party of Canada. It was not issued by the Social Credit group in the House of Commons. Rather, it was issued by a committee appointed by the Vancouver board of trade, and it does something that many post-war reconstruction reports have not done, in that it analyses the reasons for our trouble. It shows the defects [DOT] that exist in our present economic and political system. It diagnoses the trouble and then prescribes the remedy. Before the submission concludes, a series of resolutions is presented for consideration. I state this in passing, because I am certain that the committee who worked hard and long on this problem-for they must have done so-have submitted something that I believe will solve Canada's problems in the post-war period.
Many reconstruction submissions which I have read dealt with certain things that Canada might do, what could be built and so on. Submissions have been made, especially to the reconstruction committee of parliament, as to the roads that could be built, the number of bridges that could be constructed, the number of irrigation schemes and what-not that could be carried out. The report of the Vancouver board of trade says ' nothing about that, it simply asks a fundamental question, how are you going to do these things? This report deals with a question which I have failed to see answered in any other submissions I have read so far.
I remarked a little while ago that it is strange that there are so many reports being submitted. I think the reason is to be found in the history of the past number of years, perhaps the last ten or fifteen. We all recognize that there was something wrong with what is termed to-day to be the hungry thirties. We all saw ourselves pass from a period of depression into a period of apparent prosperity. I do not know that Canada has ever had such financial prosperity as she has to-day.
People are now saying the obvious thing- it has been asked hundreds of times-"You could not find the money for peace, but you can now find it for war." I do not believe that any government from this day on will be able to offer the excuse that they do not Iqjow from where they can get the money. If ever the question arises again, surely the people of Canada will be wise enough to know that that answer or that excuse will not hold.
There is one little observation I should like to make right here. There seems to be the unanswerable question of why we had such a period of poverty in the midst of plenty. I have never heard any politician answer that; I have never seen an answer by any professors of the old school of economics. The fact of the matter is that the bygone, orthodox financial expert has not yet answered that one question. The Prime Minister has not answered it. Upon analysing his speech I believe I can come to the conclusion that successful reconstruction depends upon whether or not we can sell our goods abroad. If my logic serves me as I think it should, my other conclusion is that the only reason why we had a depression then was that we could not sell our goods abroad. I am not making that statement; that is the conclusion I come to from what the Prime Minister seems to have said the other day. I do not believe that is the reason at all. I believe the only reason why
Department of Reconstruction

we had those hungry thirties, the only reason why we lived in poverty when abundance abounded, was that the government refused to adjust its monetary policy in order that the goods that were available could be distributed adequately to the people of this country.
It always seems strange to me that apparently we have sufficient brains in Canada to tackle almost every problem except the one of finance. The other night Lieutenant Commander Todd gave members of the House of Commons a lecture on the invasion. I could not help feeling at the time that behind that huge fleet, that huge army and that huge air force were the brains that so strategically managed the whole campaign as to have it meet with the success it did. I thought of the genius that must have been behind it all. I think it is one of the greatest wonders of history. Yet we know that this genius is not confined to those who hold the rank of admiral, general or air marshal. Surely there is some intelligence in Canada. Are we to admit that we can solve every other problem but that of the distribution of our goods and services to bring our country to a place where it will have the highest standard of living possible in this world? Surely no one will deny that we have the genius for that. Surely it must be somewhere. Surely that problem is not beyond solution.
I should like to refer to Hansard of June 20 when the Prime Minister spoke on this debate, and analyse one or two of the remarks he made and attempt to point out some of the matters which I think need a little criticism and some others which need a little clarification. As reported at page 3980 of Hansard the Prime Minister recognizes that there is an aspect of reconstruction which might be termed economic reconstruction. In referring to this type of reconstruction he said:
That has to do largely with the transforming of industry from malcing war supplies to making goods for human consumption and with restoring and increasing the capital equipment of the nation, together with the provision of employment for those who are being transferred from the one activity to the other. It is in connection with this economic reconstruction that the new Department of Reconstruction of the federal government will be primarily concerned.
The only reference of the Prime Minister to economic reconstruction is in connection with the transference over to a peace-time industry that will supply goods for human consumption. There is one thing sadly lacking in what I would term to be a description of economic reconstruction. Surely, if there is anything that needs to be reconstructed in order to get a vast amount of peace-time goods to our people, it is our financial arrangement which

has never been able to do it. We have had the goods; we have the railways; we have the trucks and we have been able to get the goods right up to the retailer, but we have never been able to get them from the retailer to the larders and parlours and bedrooms of our homes. That is one thing that has been lacking in our economic system. If economic reconstruction is to mean anything, it must solve that one vital problem.
The Prime Minister is at the head of the present government, and surely what he says should be taken as having some authority as far as the Liberal administration is concerned. In all that speech there was not a single solitary stand taken or statement made as to what economic change must take place-actual economic change-actual change in monetary or fiscal policy-not a single suggestion.
I go along a little farther and here, at the top of page 3981 of Hansard the Prime Minister is dealing with markets, and repeating what he said a few days ago:
Markets must be found and retained for our greatly increased food production unless we are not to face an agricultural depression.
Then farther on he says:
First and foremost-
I want you, Mr. Speaker, to get those words.
First and foremost there is the obligation to ensure the establishment of what may be most effective in the way of world organization for peace.
Then, after saying that this comes under the Department of External Affairs he says:
Probably more than any other single question requiring attention in the post-war period will be the securing of wider markets and the extension of trade.
That may sound very well and good to the man who may not be thoroughly alert. But let me ask this question. Suppose this country is not able to gain the foreign markets that we require in order to sell our surplus goods- and no one is so foolish as to believe that every' other country in the world will not be looking for the same thing, so that it will be the same old story over and over again and we shall find that foreign markets will not solve our problems for they never have before, not in this modern age, and I do not believe they ever will again-suppose we are unable to get the foreign markets we require, then what? There is absolutely no answer, Mr. Speaker. I repeat, then what? No answer.

speechtext:
As some one has said, if people have to suffer in the post-war world, if they have not suffered enough already, it is their God-given right to suffer more. But we do not want them to. We believe that there is a solution of this problem and that that solution is not to be found in foreign markets. I am not saying that we do not want foreign trade, but I say that there is much ado made about this foreign trade business. It seems strange, does it not, that we have to feed the world before we ourselves can eat? But that seems to be the philosophy held by a lot of people who talk so much about foreign trade.
The Prime Minister in his speech also made considerable mention of cooperation by the provinces with the federal government. I shall read this one passage from his speech as reported at page 3981 of Hansard, where he said:
In times of peace, on the other hand, we have to strive, in carrying out any policy, to get the good will and effective cooperation of every province, as well as carrying out our own work. I hope and. believe, as a result of what has happened during the past five years, and of the cooperation which the federal government has had in large measure from the provincial governments, that following conferences still to be held between the provinces and ourselves we shall be able to work out some means whereby we can, in the period after the war, secure still greater cooperation for the benefit of all.
I do not know whether I am right in reading between the lines there, but I should like to make sure to-night that the Prime Minister is not putting the responsibility for this whole post-war picture on the shoulders of the provinces. I hope he has not in mind here that if one or two provinces refuse to accept his proposals at the forthcoming dominion-provincial conference he will turn around and say: We will see what the country has to say about this. That would be an extremely good excuse for bringing the representatives of the provinces here.' I trust that the Prime Minister has no such motive.
I wish to say this in connection with provincial governments. The more that power is taken away from provincial governments and put into the hands of a powerful central government, the more is power taken away
from the people. Let that be stated in unequivocal terms. The fact of the matter is that you get nearer to the people when you get out to their local governments. The more that provincial governments take responsibility away from the municipal governments, the more is power taken out of the hands of the people. I say this, too. When the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) the other night brought into the picture the Rowell-Sirois report which one or two provinces refused to accept, the tenor of his argument was that there was no cooperation. Well, why not? Simply because the Rowell-Sirois report to all intents and purposes would have placed more power in the hands of a centralized government and taken it away from the hands of the people, and one or two provinces would not bow down to that sort of thing. The strange thing about the Rowell-Sirois report, which in the end would have established more centralized power and more centralized control, is that it had every banker and every chamber of commerce behind it, and they sent out their literature and arguments to the various boards of trade which did not know what it was all about and which followed in father's footsteps. All the big chain newspapers were for the Rowell-Sirois report and all the big industrialists and, without mentioning any names, a good many politicians were also for it. I say that if this government at the forthcoming dominion-provincial conference attempts to take power away from the provinces, this group is going to stand by the provinces in their argument to retain their power for the reason that their power is more abundantly the people's power.
Let me ask this question. I do not suppose I shall get an answer but it does not make any difference. The central government, namely the government here at Ottawa, have complete control of our monetary system; at any rate they are supposed to have; no other government has it. Am I to be told that this government will not receive the cooperation of the provincial governments if it says to them, "We will see that you get all the money necessary to make financially possible what is physically possible and desirable in your province"? If the government said that, does anybody believe that the provinces would not cooperate? Certainly they would; there is no doubt about that. It is all a question of whether the dominion government is willing- I am not going to say "able"-to make financially possible that which is physically possible.
The other evening, while the Prime Minister was speaking, the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) interrupted him-

Department oj Reconstruction
rightly so, I believe-by asking him where he was to get the money; was he to get it without increasing our debt? I am not going to enter at this time into all the Prime Minister's argument; but I ask him if, some time when he goes home and cannot sleep very well at night, he will turn to page 3987 of Hansard and analyse his answer. He went all the way round but he never touched the question. Finally he wound up his explanation by talking about a man having a family and, of course, he would need a home, and of course the home would have to be furnished, and so on. But is that a new condition which has suddenly come upon the scene of this world's economy? It seems to me that that has always been the case. Was it not so in the hungry thirties; was it not even so in the days of those two renowned people known as Adam and Eve? Is this part of a new idea? Is this part of the new order? I should like him to read what he said. I quote from Hansard, at page 3988:
That is the way progress is made, through demands which arise from conditions of peace and prosperity;-
Let me ask him, how can a man make a demand if he has not the money? I know the Prime Minister has studied this subject, and I am positive he knows there is never enough money coming out of industry to buy back all the goods it produces. The Prime Minister continued:
-and where you get demands of the kind which lead to the fuller employment of labour I do not think my hon. friend need fear about the increase of the public debt or taxation. . . .
Imagine that! The only answer is, "My hon. friend does not need to fear." speechtext:
I should like to associate myself with the ideas expressed by the speaker who has just taken
his seat (Mr. Hansell) and with the observations of the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Kuhl). I have listened to this debate and to the other discussions on reconstruction and to what is called the new order, and all that it amounts to, so far as I can see, is that everybody is to be put to work. If there is anything new in work, I do not know what it is. Surely work is the oldest order in the world. But when the state undertakes to put everyone to work that is new; it is state socialism, and it does not matter whether it originates on that side of the house or in that corner of the house. It is state socialism just the same and you are all going the same road.	.
The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), referring to the hon. member for Jasper-Edson, made this statement:
Our people will not want to subscribe bo the doctrine of the hon. member for Jasper-Edson.
. . . Our people believe in the dignity of work.
Exactly. Well, is there any dignity in slavery? ' Is there any dignity in work performed by a man who is compelled to work, unless from natural causes? If there is, then surely slavery was the noblest institution we have witnessed, and the slave was the noblest of mankind. We know, however, it is not so. Natural dictatorship and the struggle against it is an ennobling thing; nobody denies that. But the Almighty, or Providence, has permitted mankind through science and so forth, to make it possible to lift the burden of a struggle for mere existence from the backs of mankind. And when human beings step in and presume to take the place of the Almighty and to say to men, "You shall work or starve," that is dictatorship and it does not matter whether it is called Liberalism, Progressive-Conservatism, C.C.F.ism or Tim Buckism. It is all the same and it all originates from the same idea, or philosophy. What differentiates not only our group but our movement throughout the world, particularly in the British empire, the movement known as social credit? It is this. We believe in voluntary effort. We believe that the time has come when it is no longer necessary to impose a struggle upon everyone for the bare necessities of life. That has been solved. Struggle there must be, but the struggle should be lifted to a higher plane than the mere struggle for existence. We have always advocated dividends for all and that has been ridiculed. First of all, the question was raised, where would the money come from? Well, at the present time over fifty per cent of the production of this country and of our allies is being given-I say given because it is given in the form of munitions-to Germany
Department oj Reconstruction

and our other enemies. That is a national or if you prefer, an international dividend. We ask nothing in exchange. As a consequence of that, even though the cream of the nation is either in uniform or in munition factories, while essential retail goods and the necessities of life are being produced by the very young and the very old, in spite of that fact, and that we are giving away over fifty per cent of our production, right out of the country, the present standard of living in Canada is higher than ever before.
I know there are certain inconveniences and restrictions, but I think I am right in saying that, if you average Canada right through, the present standard of living is higher than it ever was before. Certainly it is a great deal higher than it was for the ten years preceding the war. The reason for that is surely obvious. The problem of marketing has been solved. There is no trouble about marketing and therefore there is no trouble about producing. And if you solve the problem of' consumption you automatically solve the problem of production. I might say, in passing, that the paying of a dividend is not new. Not only is the idea of it not new, but as an actual fact it is not new. I have here a book entitled, "Monetary Experiments", by Richard A. Lester, and in a foreword by Professor Kemmerer the following appears:
This study is_ one of a series being published under the auspices of the international finance section of the Department of Economics and Social Institutions in Princeton university.
This book is published under the auspices of the university of Princeton, and in the chapter headed, "Social Dividend in Maryland", I read:
^When Maryland first issued paper money in 1733 most of it was given away-a certain sum to each inhabitant over fifteen years of age. This was done in order that the paper money might be "the more useful to the inhabitants" and its circulation might be "as speedy and diffusive as possible." The legislature hoped by this means "to remove the difficulties under which the inhabitants had long laboured." In a sense this was a sort of "social dividend" similar to that advocated by Major C. H. Douglas in his books on social credit.
At the end of the chapter there are a few words which sum up the experiment, and they are as follows:
From his detailed study of forty-five years of money in Maryland, Professor Gould concludes: "Considering the peculiar benefits to grain and tobacco culture, the conveniences offered to trade, and the faithful redemption of every shilling at face value, it is hardly too much to say that this was the most successful paper money issued by any of the colonies."
It can be seen that the national dividend is not even new; this was done before and it
fMr. Jaques.]
was a great success. To those who, like the hon. member for Essex East and others, have been so fond of saying that it would demoralize and pauperize the people, I would say that it was the recipients of that dividend who a few years afterwards fought and won the war of independence.
I shall now quote a few lines from Douglas himself. He has this to say on state socialism:
State socialism is based on the premise that, firstly, the control of policy is resident in administration, and, secondly, that it is possible to "socially" control administration, and thirdly, that the state should be able to supply economic pressure to the individual; whereas I suggest to you that the control of policy is resident in credit, and its financial derivations, of which money is one, while administration is a technical and expert matter not susceptible of being socialized, and, lastly, that the only possible method by which the highest civilization can be reached is to make it impossible for either the state or any other body to apply economic pressure to any individual.
That is tbe reason for the dividend. *It should be obvious to any thinking person that the world is coming to the parting of the ways. People speak of a new order. We believe in a new order. A new order should mean individual freedom. After centuries of struggle we have won political freedom but the world has not yet won individual economic freedom. The only offer that I have any knowledge of from any other movement but our own is this: People are being offered economic security at the price of individual freedom. That is what they are being offered. That is what they were offered and received in Germany, Russia and Italy. That is what they are being offered to-day not only in Canada but throughout the British empire. The so-called new order is state socialism. It is based, not on individual freedom as it should be, but on collective security at the price of individual freedom.
Quite recently the hon. member for Jasper-Edson was criticized for a statement he made about the leisure state. We well know that there is no room for a leisure state in war time. That is one of the reasons why war is hell. There is no leisure. But surely after the war is over and when the worst of the damage of the war and the waste of war have been repaired we should look to the ideal of a new order, and that should be toward a leisure state and not a work state; that is, work for the sake of working. Major Douglas has this to say on that subject:
The more the maintenance of life can be shifted from the backs of men on to the backs of machines, the more important it is to find a creative outlet for the human energy released, and the more certain is it that a considerable portion of this energy will, without compulsion,

Department oj Reconstruction
be devoted to the improvement of the industrial machines. That is to say, that if a practical policy based on these considerations be pursued there will be a fall in the man-hours required for routine or operating work, and a consequent rise in the man-hours available for design and research work. The industrial machine is a lever continuously being lengthened by progress which enables the burden of Atlas to be lifted with ever-increasing ease. As the number of men required to work the lever decreases, so the number of men set free to lengthen it increases.
I shall read one more quotation from Major Douglas on the leisure state. It is as follows:
If we assume that the constant effort to reduce the amount of labour per unit of production are justified, and we recognize the unquestionable fact that the genuine consumption capacity of the individual is limited, we _must recognize that the world, whether consciously or not, is working towards the leisure state. The production system under this conception would be required to produce those goods and services which the consumer desires of it with a minimum and probably decreasing amount of human labour. Production, and still more the activities which are commonly referred to as business, would of necessity cease to be the major interest of life and would, as has happened to so many biological activities, be relegated to a position of minor importance.
This movement of social credit is a great deal more than a mere method of finance. Monetary reform is not enough. Social credit is a philosophy of life, and the financial part of it is merely the means to gain the ends of the policy. The basic philosophy of social credit is freedom for the individual.
There are only two methods of production in the world-there can only be two-compulsion and persuasion. So far, the world has been more or less under persuasion. If there has been compulsion it has been imposed by Providence, by God or by Nature, whichever you prefer. But that has been overcome, and now we are threatened with production by compulsion-a compulsion imposed, not by nature, but by individuals who have assumed powers which, rightly, belong only to the Almighty. That is, in my opinion, the essence of all dictatorships.
We propose that everybody should be guaranteed-every man, woman and child-at least the necessities of life, whether they work or not. I do not mean to say that this would apply, of course, in war time and probably for some time after the war; but it is an ideal to guide us. All work would be voluntary, and that would be a noble thing. As I said before, I see nothing noble in being compelled by the state to work at a task which one must accept or starve. That condition is all right when it is imposed by nature. But that condition we have overcome; the problem is no longer one of production. As every speaker has said, consciously or otherwise, the problem is to market, to sell, if you like, or to distribute what we now can produce in such large quantities.
Therefore there is no longer any reason why all work should not be put on a voluntary basis. We could begin, of course, by lowering the age for pensions, and increasing the amounts. Perhaps we could raise the age for the education of youth. We could shorten the working time at both ends. The ideal should be toward a leisure state, with work freely done and not imposed by a dictator.
I hope hon. members will not deliberately distort what is said by members in this group.
I suppose there is not a member in the house who has a family who does not regard it as his duty-and rightly so-to leave his family as financially independent as possible. I am sure that would be the first care and the first instinct of every father and mother in the house. If that is right, then surely that is the very best thing we can desire for our own children. Therefore, in the long run, it must be the very best thing for all children, and all people.
Of course it has never been possible, 60 long as the world was in a state of real scarcity. But in this day and age, when as a result of the war we shall have immensely increased our powers of production, the problem will not be one of production but, as has been said so often, one of markets. Some say that we shall have to give away to foreign countries a great portion of our production, through a favourable balance of trade and foreign lending-which is the same thing as giving.
I believe that charity begins at home; and if it is necessary-and I am sure it is-to give away part of our production, because there is no other way of getting rid of it, then I contend that we should set a good example in our own country and pay ourselves some dividends. If we did that, it would not be long before the world would follow our example.

Mr. Speaker, the word "reconstruction" is given a wide meaning in the interpretation section of the bill. It includes every undertaking by dominion, provincial or municipal authority or by any corporation or other person that may contribute to the reorganization of industry, in order to provide maximum production and full employment during and following the change-over from war-time production of industry to peace-time production.
I should like to take the opportunity this definition affords me to bring to the attention of the house very briefly a matter which I
Department of Reconstruction

believe is of importance, if some of our reconstruction and interprovincial problems are to be considered and dealt with intelligently. It has to do with the lack of reliable information available respecting trade between the provinces.
If I were to ask the bureau of statistics for figures showing the trade between New Brunswick and Saskatchewan, or between any one province and any other province, the information would not be available. The bureau of statistics does not have such information. It seems to me it is important that such records should be kept, if we are to have a true picture of interprovincial business. Unless we have those records, it is impossible intelligently to study and discuss some of the economic problems and reconstruction problems which will arise after the war. Until such information is available we shall be travelling in the dark, and it will be impossible for us to obtain a true picture of Canada's interprovincial business. I am informed that this information could be obtained by the bureau of statistics and that it would not be difficult to obtain, although it would involve an additional expenditure of about $10,000 a year.
On April 7, 1926, the governor in council appointed Sir Andrew Rae Duncan, the Hon. W. B. Wallace, then judge of the county court of district No. 1, in the province of Nova Scotia, and Professor Cyrus Macmillan, Master of Arts and Doctor of Philosophy of McGill university, to be commissioners under the Inquiries Act for the purpose of conducting an inquiry into the conditions and claims of the people of the maritime provinces and to make such specific recommendations as in the opinion of the commissioners would result in affording relief from the conditions complained of. Mr. F. Maclure Sclanders, commissioner of the Saint John board of trade, acted as secretary of the commission.
The commission's report is dated September 23, 1926, and in it the commissioners urged that a system of statistics should be made regularly available from as early a date as possible on the trade of the maritime provinces with other provinces and with foreign markets as well. Section 39 of the report deals with this matter, and I should like to read the first and third paragraphs thereof. The first paragraph reads:
We have had brought before us the lack of any comprehensive measurement of the trade of the maritime provinces with other provinces and with foreign markets. We were ourselves disappointed not to be able to pursue investigations on trade matters along lines which such statistics would have enabled us to do. We found on inquiry at the dominion bureau of

statistics that consideration had been given some time ago to this very subject but, mainly through lack of organization in the statistics relating to certain phases of transportation, it was not possible to proceed with the plans that had been formulated. We strongly urge that these difficulties should be overcome, as they can be, and that on this phase of internal trade a system of statistics should be made regularly available from as early a date as possible.
The third paragraph reads:
With regard to the general function of the bureau of statistics, we venture to draw attention to the importance of providing a comprehensive statistical organization in a country situated as is Canada with a series of provinces differing often in economic outlook. Very considerable progress has already been made in this direction, but we feel the bureau could be increased in efficiency by being given improved facilities for the kind of organization it is necessary to develop as an independent central agency covering the activities of all departments from the statistical side.
It has been suggested that the reason why this recommendation was not put into force was that representatives in the house from Ontario and Quebec objected because it would show the trade among the provinces to be in their favour. I do not consider that is the real reason, because I have always found members of the house from Ontario and Quebec ready and willing to give a sympathetic hearing to the other provinces in order to endeavour to find a solution of their difficulties.
Until statistics on this trade are obtainable we shall be travelling in the dark. It is not possible for us to obtain a true picture of our interprovincial affairs or to make an intelligent study of them until these figures are made available to us. I ask the government to implement this provision of the Duncan report and to take steps to see that statistics of trade between the different provinces are made available.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to this debate with regard to the setting up of a Department of Reconstruction. The more I have heard, the more it has become apparent to me that reconstruction is largely an engineering problem. I happen to be an engineer, and perhaps I can take some of the time of the house to express a few views which are diametrically opposed to some of those expressed by my hon. friends to my extreme left.
The definition of an engineer has been given as a man who can do something for a dollar which it would cost two or three dollars to have done by somebody else. If an engineer is given enough time, enough money and enough men he can do practically anything. Chauncey Depew has said that, given those

Department oj Reconstruction
three things, he could build a railroad to the north pole. Many of the plans that have been discussed in this house and have received publicity in the public press more or less fall into the category of building a railroad to the north pole. They seem to be very fine in debate and they look all right on paper; but having lived all over the world, having made my living in several countries besides Canada, perhaps I may be excused when I say that a great deal of what has been said is impracticable.
I am going to deal directly with the financial set-up, which has been mentioned in this house at considerable length. If we look at the beginning of chaos in the world we shall see that the first inevitable step toward this war -started with the so-called managed currencies. We have the statement of Sir John Anderson in England that the beginning of Great Britain's chaos was with the adoption of the gold standard. That, I submit, is wholly inaccurate. With all due respect to Sir John Anderson, I take issue with him. England returned to the gold standard on the basis of the pre-war price of $20.67 an ounce, with a tremendously inflated currency and a tremendously inflated national debt. To say that that was a return to the gold standard is technically correct, but actually it was a return to an exchange standard between paper currency and metal which could not work because the paper was so tremendously inflated. That is the situation with regard to the adoption of the gold standard in England. Let us see what happened.
Despite everything that has been said, we in this country depend, whether anybody likes it or not, for our prosperity upon international trade, and when the war is over we shall depend for our prosperity a great deal more upon international trade. One fundamental about international trade, particularly forward trade, is that the buyer and the seller can deal in a standard whose value will remain ' constant when the contract is carried out. Throughout the centuries that has been the fundamental rule of success in international trade. Nothing has altered; nothing will alter.
We see that to-day we have a managed currency. All currencies are managed, fictitiously managed, with relation to the price of gold. In the United States they will purchase gold but not sell it at $35 an ounce, but on the free gold market both in Alexandria and in Bombay gold to-day sells for somewhat over $70 an ounce. The house may consider this an academic question but it is far from it. It means that the great bulk of the people with whom we shall have to trade, the great centres of population which are in the orient still have
hard currencies. They believe and throughout years of bitter strife they have found it true that gold is the one thing they can trust to and to-day, despite the fact that large sums of United States currency are circulating in the orient through the American troops, United States currency is at a very great discount and the Americans have had to resort, so I understand, to two types of currency known as the blue seal and the yellow seal.
The pound sterling is an internal currency except in the controlled parts of the sterling block to-day. Its value outside England is extremely variable. Special invasion currency was issued for the attack in Normandy. I mention this because the United States dollar and the pound sterling are to-day, in the minds of the great centres of population in the orient, losing their intrinsic value because they are not convertible into a metallic base. Those are the facts. We may or may not like them. But all history shows that experiment after experiment has been made in fiat money from the time of Marcus Aurelius right down to the present day and it has inevitably brought chaos.
I mention this, Mr. Speaker, because I have lived in two countries where managed currency led to inflation, where I saw great poverty and tremendous distress caused by the printing press. One of those countries was Germany and the other Brazil. One of them after the last war was poverty-stricken; or the Germans said they were. The other country was Brazil, rich in natural resources. Both suffered from inflation, and the people, the workers, were the ones who suffered. I want to make that very clear because I have experienced inflation in those two countries and I know what it means.
It is said that the Americans have or had a hoard of gold which would never be of any use to them. But in the last three months the United States treasury has lost in the neighbourhood of $166,000,000 of gold for external purposes, and that despite the imports and the purchases she has made from Canada and other gold-producing countries which sell to the United States. Furthermore, their gold currency coverage which was over ninety per cent a year ago has dropped to slightly over sixty per cent and it may now be less than that. That is what is happening to the American gold. The American gold is one of the most useful assets the United States has ever had, as was our gold at the beginning of the war, as was admitted by Mr. Graham Towers, who said that Canada's gold saved Canada's bacon in the first year of the war.
Department of Reconstruction

We talk about divorcing ourselves from managed currency and having the printed dollar. If I thought it would work, I would advocate it.

That was not the way by which the pioneers of Canada built up this country; and we are to-day, because of the peculiar idea that we can live on the state, headed either for state socialism or chaos.
Mr. HARRY R. JACKMAN (Rosedale): Mr. Speaker, in rising to support the bill by which the Department of Reconstruction will be set up, I cannot be certain, nor do I suppose any hon. member can be absolutely certain whether it will have any great usefulness. It may result in merely a fact-collection agency; and its usefulness or otherwise cannot be foretold in advance of the events which will follow upon victory in this war.
Nevertheless, this Department of Reconstruction may perform a useful purpose, and with that possibility in view I am glad to support it and to advance certain suggestions to which I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) might give consideration.
It may well be that when victory is assured to us we shall find that our job will not be to provide work for people; on the other hand it may be a job for the government to put a damper on an incipient boom. We have, stored up in the hands of the people, a tremendous amount of savings, much of which cannot be spent at the present time because there are not civilian goods on which to spend them, and we shall see what will be the result, when the war is over, of this great unleashed amount of money which is available for consumer goods. It is, however, well to be in readiness in case there is unemployment and it is necessary to stimulate production and consumption in this country, and it may, therefore, be that the Department of Reconstruction will have a useful and important purpose to serve. In any event, the readjustment and rehabilitation will not be automatic, even if the natural demand for workers is sufficient to absorb all those who are willing to offer their services in the industrial, and agricultural and mining fields of this country. However, that natural demand, if it is sufficiently great to absorb them all, is not likely to be facilitated or expedited by the setting up of this department. There is bound to be a time lag between the rehabilitation and the demobilization of the men and women from our forces and from our industries before they are placed in civilian goods industries.
As I understand it, it is not the policy of the present government to create jobs, either through public works or other expenditures

Department of Reconstruction
of public moneys, if the natural working of the economic system is sufficient to give our people employment. One does not know whether the ministry of reconstruction will become a mere repository and exchange of information having to do with jobs, or whether it may have a general overriding power over other departments of the government which are specifically charged with carrying on certain projects. It will undoubtedly face a delicate position, because it will have a great deal to do, if it does have any function to perform at all, with other departments of the government and also with departments of provincial governments.
For example, the Department of Reconstruction would undoubtedly know about the amount of money and the amount of manpower involved in government projects of one kind or another. It would also likely know of the amount of money and manpower involved in the major private undertakings throughout the country. But I do not see how it could possibly know of the millions of private projects which will be undertaken by our citizens, whether they be the building of homes or the purchase of durable articles. That information, which is of the greatest importance, cannot be known or even estimated with any reasonable degree of accuracy by a department of reconstruction, and to some extent, perhaps to a very large extent, that deficiency will vitiate the work of the department itself. How is the department to know how individuals are going to spend their money? Will they spend it on homes or on autos, on taking out a new insurance policy or on a vacation, or will they, because of lack of confidence in the immediate future after the war, decide to hold whatever cash or victory bonds they have and refuse to spend their savings and thus take that money out of circulation?
What I should like to emphasize particularly is that the government should indicate what is to be the driving or motivating force in our workaday life in the post-war period, what is to be the machinery which, as they say makes the clock tick. Are we to have government direction and regimentation, being told what to do and unwilling to do more than our assigned tasks because there is no reward or incentive to do more than the minimum? Or are we to operate as free men under rules and regulations which are imposed by the government but which will guarantee opportunity and fairness to all our people? The answer to that problem strikes at the great question which confronts us all, as to whether we are to have a socialist state
in Canada, or whether we shall operate under the system of free enterprise and individual initiative.
To-day the market is provided by the government for all our agricultural and industrial production. The government pays the whole bill and provides the incentive through paying whatever is necessary to produce the goods. There is little regard to cost, as we see by the evidence in the war expenditures committee, where some shipyards produce a 10,000-ton freighter at one price and others at a higher price. The important thing in fighting a war is to get production. Costs mean little and profits or earnings less. You must produce the goods in order to win the war, and whatever consequences fall in the wake of that must be considered in the later period and not while the fighting is going on.
Fortunately, the financial and economic system has been strong enough to stand the strain to date, and although we live and learn, speaking in terms perhaps of years, we do not know how much longer the system can stand the strain which is at present imposed upon it with the steadily mounting debt and the charges and other regulations attendant thereon. If we do not have a regimented, totalitarian state, then we shall have a free economy where every man will be his own master, able to choose the vocation or job which he wishes. May I point out particularly to the house that the greatest stumbling block to a return to the system of free economy is the present taxation and fiscal policy of the country. No better means could have been devised to bring about a socialist state than the present taxation policies of Canada, and if they Sre continued there is no question that free enterprise and initiative will expire.
At the outbreak of the war, taxation was used as the instrument to stifle civilian production, which was literally choked off. Certainly there should not be an increase in civilian production brought to the market to any greater extent than will enable our people to live in a reasonable degree of comfort. Certainly there should be no increase in standards. Wages were stabilized in civilian industries but certainly not in war plants, where workers were doing jobs at higher rates and war plants were attracting workers from ordinary fields of industry. We have only to look at the aircraft industry to find a typical example of the process. That was all to the good. But the reverse situation will obtain in the post-war period. No longer do we want- to strangle civilian production. On the contrary, we want to cancel all war production and to turn all our man-power to production
Department of Reconstruction

for civilian use. We shall turn from production to kill to production to live. It is, therefore, logical that we should reverse the process which we adopted at the outbreak of the war whereby we raised taxes to prohibitive levels, particularly on business, and to a large extent on individuals also.
Unless that is done, initiative and the motivating force which we have always had in a system of free economy will be lost to us and we shall lose that freedom which so many of us prize. At the present time the minimum tax on business is forty per cent; if that business earns more than the average earnings during the 1936-1939 period, the tax is 100 per cent; then whatever is left after that may be distributed to the shareholders, and they are taxed in their particular brackets at anywhere from thirty per cent to ninety-eight per cent. So that it does not take more than simple arithmetic to realize that there is no possible incentive for one to engage in business or to expand, or even for an individual who is not in business or corporation brackets to earn more money, because the brackets are so high that it is not worth the extra effort.
We find that not only in the upper brackets, whether they are connected with the war effort or not, is it no longer profitable to do this, but workers in the factories do not find it profitable to work the sixth day because that puts them in the higher brackets for the whole week's wages and there is so little left of the sixth day's wages that it is not worth while working. The consequence is that the nation loses production, and the Department of National Revenue loses what it might otherwise have obtained had the taxation been more reasonable.
It may be that such a system is necessary- I will not say that it is, but this is not the place to debate the question-during a period of war, but certainly during peace time and during the great conversion period after the war we must not have such conditions obtaining. There is nothing more important for the Prime Minister to announce than the government's intention with regard to post-war taxation; for the power to tax is the power to destroy, and that is what is happening as far, as civilian production, particularly new production, is concerned. And rightly so, at the present time, because we have a war to carry on and we do not want more goods for civilian use. But companies as well as individuals must know whether they will be compensated for the risk they have to undertake and the enterprise and management they must con' tribute in the post-war period, and particularly is this so of new businesses.
{Mr. Jackman.]
Some government officials have left the impression that it would be their recommendation that taxes after the war should be substantially reduced. We are all aware that the treasury will need revenue in the post-war period, but it would be foolish to kill the goose that lays the golden eggs. People must know where they stand in the matter of taxation. While the question is important to all, it is of the greatest importance to those who are engaged in business to provide leadership through w-hich jobs are created. Canadian citizens not government departments are going to do the major planning in this country, and it is time to think now of the deciding factor of post-war taxation; otherwise there is no use in having government commissions and boards and other public bodies set up to decide how much work can be created, how many jobs can be provided, how much capital expansion there may be. What we need is a clear chart so that business will know whether it can undertake new things and whether there is sufficient incentive for them, because unless there is some compensation for the risk involved there is not likely to be much go ahead; the green light is not likely to come on as far as business is concerned.
It is not necessary to bring to the attention of the house this fact, that not only does a nation perish without vision but that without leadership the nation is lost. We must, therefore, provide a chart whereby leaders in business and industry can guide their future plans, and a fair and equitable taxation policy applicable to the post-war period should be announced immediately. Let us know what our ascertainable post-war expenditures are likely to be. Let us know the over-all picture of social welfare costs. Inasmuch as it is in our power to provide it, let us give the people what they want and what they need. But it is also our duty to tell them what the cost is and how that cost is to be borne by our people. Reconstruction means reemployment and job creation. That is what the people want, not doles and hand-outs, even if it is their own money. Let us provide a fair day's wage for a fair day's work. Public ownership may well be desirable in some instances, but where there is room for competition and development let not the government become a limiting monopoly. For example, in the air transport field we find the present government-excluding any likely competition even when the whole world is our oyster and there is plenty of room for not only the government line but for a number of competitors in what is likely to prove one of the greatest and fastest expanding fields of transportation.

Department oj Reconstruction
Has this government for one moment considered what the effect already is on young Canadians with competing air transport companies? Are they likely to continue to engage in air transportation in Canada with the de-. vitalizing hand of a limiting monopoly apparently to be laid on this great industry of promise? Is it any wonder that the brightest of our young men, those who would provide leadership in the field, are already being attracted to the United States where there are no less than half a dozen companies engaged in international transportation? If we are to have a real reconstruction policy in this country, let us not adopt halfway measures and for want of political courage fall between the two stools of national socialism and free enterprise, If we are to have an incentive and not just to obey orders, let this government announce its post-war taxation policy; for how can business which creates jobs be bold and forward-looking if it does not know the environment in which it is to operate? With the war providing a sure market for the proceeds of industry and agriculture there has been little business risk The taxation policy may have been rigorous but not unsound in principle. After victory, with production to satisfy the needs and desires of millions of our people, with all its attendant risk and the necessity of finding markets, let the government proclaim a fair system of post-war taxation for all, so that consumers will have money to buy and producers some incentive to go ahead and take the risk and produce.
If the government is interested in reconstruction as are all our people, and particularly those of the armed forces and in war industries let it announce without delay the conditions under which business will be called upon in the post-war period to carry on.

I am sure
that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has reason to have a feeling of satisfaction at the general acceptance of this bill by the house. I should not have taken part in the debate at this time had it not been for some remarks made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). Fearing that I might be called to order if I attempted to deal with his remarks when the bill comes before the house I take this occasion to reply to my hon. friend.
Not only is the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar running true to form in his actions on this measure but also in the actions of those who surround him when they speak on matters of which they have no knowledge. The general social programme that was inaugurated by the Liberal party many years ago had its
beginning long years before there were any Cooperative Commonwealth-Federation members in this house. And this includes such measures as old age pensions, with which the hon. member attempted to deal. I wish to refer to old age pensions particularly. Hon. members in that corner of the house have frequently taken unto themselves the entire credit for having instituted and, as they frequently put it, forced old1 age pensions through this house and upon the leaders of of that day. As a matter of fact, they had as much to do with the formulation and passage of old age pensions as had the mummies of Egypt.
I am sorry that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) is not in his place at the moment, because for the first time that I can recall they have given him credit for having had some part in bringing about the passage of old age pensions. That is quite true, but the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was overgenerous that evening. However, what is the history of old age pensions? I distinctly recall the seven members-I have the names here-who met in a room on the fifth floor in the latter stages of the session of 1922. Who were the seven members? They were as follows :	George G. Coote, the then member
for Macleod; T. W. Bird, the then member for Nelson; Henry E. Spencer, the then member for Battle River; Miss Agnes C. MacPhail, the then member for Southeast Grey; E. J. Garland, the then member for Bow River; J. S. Woodsworth, the then member for Winnipeg North Centre and W. J. Ward. These were the seven members who met in that room. Neither the then member for Winnipeg North, nor the hon. member for Comox-Albemi were present. As time went by, our organization gathered momentum; by 1923 we had gathered around us usually from twenty to twenty-five members who would meet with us, and by 1925 there were anywhere from forty to fifty members who met frequently to deal with old age pensions. And who were the forty or fifty members? Well, regularly there was a member of the Conservative party, the then member for New Westminster, and we always had a considerable number of Liberal members, but mainly they were Progressive.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar referred to a letter which was written in 1926 to our present Prime Minister and to the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, who was leading the opposition. The letter was in the form of an offer of support. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar would lead the house and the country to believe that that letter came from the then member for Winnipeg North

Department oj Reconstruction

Centre, the then member for Winnipeg North and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, which was entirely untrue. The members of the Labour party of that day were nothing more than a mere incident. Old age pensions had no particular force in so far as the two Labour members who were in the house at that time were concerned. It was the Progressive members, supported by two or three Conservative members and a number of Liberal members, but mainly Progressive members, who made old age pensions possible.
I wish to remind the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar when he speaks of the amount of $20 a month not being sufficient, that that was the amount agreed upon by Mr. Woodsworth, Mr. Heaps and all the other members at that time. Seventy years of age and $20 a month was all that was asked' for. Therefore I think it is well that we put the record straight and that the country should know who was responsible for placing old age pensions on the statute books of this country.
I should also like to refer to some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar in reply to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). Surely the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar-and he is nobody's fool-must have known the facts, or was he deliberately attempting to mislead the country, talking with tongue in his cheek.

I think many of those soldiers, too, would hope to come back to a free Canada, one where free enterprise is here, waiting for them. I could not help feeling when I read this press report of the hon. member's statement that he is not fair to Canada or to the Canadian people.

As we consider this paragraph I think it would be a good thing, to make sure that we all realize, as I think the Prime Minister does, that it involves, first, that there shall be a maximum domestic market in Canada for all the goods which will be produced in Canada or for all the
Department oj Reconstruction

goods for which our products may be exchanged. I think the Prime Minister will agree that that is a fundamental premise. There must be a maximum domestic market in Canada for all the goods produced in Canada and for the goods for which the surplus goods of Canada can be exchanged. In other words, the purchasing power in the hands of the people of Canada must be raised to a level at which they will be able to consume Canadian production to the fullest extent of their needs. That will be involved in this paragraph and I want to make sure the Prime Minister appreciates that fact. If our primary and secondary industries are to be able to carry on to the maximum of their efficiency there must be a level of purchasing power among Canadian consumers which will enable them to consume to the ultimate extent the production of Canadian industry, both primary and secondary. That is involved in this paragraph.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Full employment would mean as much in the way of employment as it is possible to achieve, but it does not necessarily mean the guarantee of employment to everyone at every hour -of the day. We must not fail to take into account such matters as seasonal unemployment and the like. But it does refer to what we ^generally consider as mass employment, the (employment of large numbers. The aim of reconstruction will be to strive to achieve the fullest possible employment from domestic and foreign trade or commerce. I do not know if I have caught the purpose of my hon. friend's question, but I am trying to answer it.

speechtext: The Prime Minister's words would indicate that he has, but I am not entirely sure that he appreciates to the full the meaning of what I said. This involves that all consumers in Canada shall be able to buy to the limit of their needs the goods which Canadian industry will be able to produce. If these words really mean what they should, that will be involved. That means that the standard of wages in Canada will be such that we shall not have a large percentage of Canadian wage earners getting less than $500 a year. That will be a condition not to be tolerated in Canada.
