My hon. friend understands that there is a difference between an objective and a guarantee. The objective is set forth here quite clearly, but I would not say that any government measure could go so far as to guarantee to individuals what their purchasing power is to be from day to day. The objective we are seeking is to enable all

classes to have a minimum standard of living. That is the government's policy with respect to reconstruction, not confining reconstruction merely to the producing of commodities and the sale of goods, but extending it to the social and economic needs of the people, and to meeting economic hazards.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
I think that is fair enough. I am going to be a little more specific. If men are to have the greatest opportunity to work in the production of shoes, then the people of Canada must be in a position to buy the maximum number of shoes that they need. The same principle would apply to all the commodities Canada is able to produce. If the people are not able to buy shoes, then people certainly are not going to be employed in producing shoes. The same is true with respect to all industries in Canada.
This means that probably we are not going to depend upon the wages which industry at present feels able to pay; we are going to find means of supplementing wages and incomes. We may even go so far as to make use of a dividend in order to enable the people to consume. I have not said much about dividends, but probably it is about time that many members of this house began to contemplate them seriously. The family allowance is an example, although that is just a meagre, halting, hesitating little device; in the light of the potential productive capacity of Canada, it- is almost contemptible. However, I think the Prime Minister deserves credit for taking a step along this line. I just wanted to make sure that the Prime Minister saw the possibilities that were involved. The paragraph reads:
"reconstruction" means the reestablishment in civil life and reemployment on demobilization of the men and women of the armed services, of persons released from war industry, and the reorganization of industry, in order to provide maximum production. . . .
You cannot have a maximum production of cheese unless every person in Canada can eat all the cheese he needs. Nor can you have a maximum production of strawberries unless everybody in Canada can have all the strawberries he needs. You can say the same about the whole list of commodities. In drafting this statement the Prime Minister has gone a long way,, provided that it can be worked out to mean just what the words should mean. This paragraph goes the full limit of social credit. I just wanted to make that clear, although I do not believe the Prime Minister had any such thing as that in mind. However, I hope he did and I thought it would be worth while to bring it up.

Department oj Reconstruction
There is another point involved here and I want to make sure that the Prime Minister agrees with this. Not only must prices of wheat, milk, beef and other primary products have a floor, but the floor must be high enough to stimulate the maximum desired production of all those commodities in Canada. This does not mean that the increased price, we will say, of beef or milk or any other primary product must be paid by the consumer. In other words, there will be a subsidy perhaps, where necessary, paid to the primary producer which might raise the price of a bushel of wheat, for example, to SI.25, whereas the consumer would have to pay only seventy-five cents a bushel. This sounds strange to orthodox ears, but it is not strange to men who see visions of the possibilities of a new order. The device has already been used in Britain of paying to primary producers seventy-five cents a dozen for eggs and letting the consumers have the eggs for fifty cents a dozen. Under a new order the difference will not be paid through taxing the people or by borrowings from the people, but will be paid with money which will represent the production of the country and will be governed only by the extent of the production of the country.
I set out to point out that this really means that prices to primary consumers will be so high as to include not only the cost of production but a fair remuneration which will justify the primary producers in going forward with a generous production programme. I presume that the Prime Minister had that in mind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
If I may refer first to the question asked by the hon. member for Cape Breton South as to whether the merchant marine is included, I was perfectly sure that it vras included. If it had been twenty-five minutes past ten o'clock on Monday morning, instead of twenty-five minutes past ten o'clock on Friday night I would have caught my hon. friend's point at once. In the definition of "industry" my hon. friend will see that transportation is included. Paragraph (b) states:
(b) "industry" includes merchandising, manufacturing . . . transportation, . . .
And so forth. He will also see that the definition of "reconstruction" includes "maximum production and full employment during and following the change over from war-time production of industry to peace-time production". So that, reading the two together, my hon. friend will see that the merchant marine is included. I felt that it would be there in one form or another. There is extra emphasis given to what relates to the armed forces.
In answer to the hon. member for Lethbridge I do catch at times what I think is his meaning. Then it sort of fades out because I catch something else from what he is putting forward. As nearly as I can gather, he is concerned that this legislation aims at maximum employment, and I agree with him in that.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: I am merely pointing out what it really involves. If the legislation is to attain actually and in fact what the wording of this paragraph implies, then a technique will be involved which will include the measures I have indicated. It will include a scientific adjustment of prices, a scientific adjustment of wages by wage bonuses, the distribution of consumers' purchasing power which will probably make the dividend advocated in Alberta look rather pale. I hope that all members on the treasury benches can get this idea without too much suffering on the part of the Canadian people, because it is the Canadian people who will suffer; it is not you men, not directly. I hope that you can get this idea before it is too late. You cannot be sure that you are going to be able to sell Canadian cheese abroad, but if you manage the economy of this country aright you can be sure that you will be able to sell in Canada all the cheese that all the Canadian people will eat. That is what is involved.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: What about wheat?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: You can sell all the wheat in Canada that all the Canadian people can eat. The same rule applies to every commodity.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: You would have a great time eating all the wheat we produce.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
I did not say that you would eat all the wheat. You will have a hard enough time getting this into your head if you take just what I say, and do not imagine things I did not say. That is one of the difficulties with a lot of men. They do not take what was said but take what they imagine was said. What is said is strong enough.
What I have to say, Mr. Chairman, is simply this, that if we take pains to see that the Canadian people have consumer purchasing power with which to absorb and use the products of our industry, both primary and secondary, at fair prices, we can be sure of that much. We cannot be sure of selling any given amount of our goods abroad. We want to sell as much as we can abroad without hurting anybody else, but we do want to make -sure of this home market. I believe that tli
Department of Reconstruction

way in. which this paragraph is worded implies all these things, but I am not at all sure that the draftsman of this bill had these things in mind.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have so far refrained from taking any part in the discussion of this bill because I felt that what I have to say could be very well said on this section. Because of the mention of casual labour by the Prime Minister I should like to draw to his attention and that of the government the position of the waterfront worker. In 1936 Canada brought into effect the national harbours board, which took 'in the *eight national harbours throughout the dominion with an investment of something like $224,000,000 A large number of men are *employed at the various ports as casual labour handling incoming and outgoing freight. On the Atlantic coast at both Halifax and Saint John these men work for something like four :to five or six months a year on the waterfront ;and they have to depend for the rest of the year on what they earn during the period they are employed. I feel that if we are to take care of labour, it is that type of employment that we must provide for. The present Minister of Labour brought into effect last year a measure under which he organized a labour pool and guaranteed a certain number of men, roughly seven hundred, a floor wage at waterfront work during the full season. I am going to suggest to the government that the national harbours board consider taking over the complete handling of freight at all ports throughout Canada. It would give the national harbour's board something definite to deal with. They deal with transportation, and the handling of incoming and outgoing freight is part of the transportation problem.
I am suggesting that, with the large investment which the government now have in national harbours throughout the dominion, they could very well take up this question of labour and guarantee the men an annual wage instead of three to six months' employment, so that the mein may be on hand at all times and able to handle freight in the most expeditious manner. They might also extend their activities by buying proper equipment for handling freight in the various ports and thustadd to the efficiency of the operations. I believe that the government would be well advised to take -over, under the jurisdiction of the national harbours board, the work of the longshoremen, the checkers, the freight handlers and all skilled and unskilled labour on the waterfront. If a plan were inaugurated whereby this could be done it would lead to greater efficiency. I would further suggest a preference such as wa3 (Mr. Blackmore.]
brought into effect by the late Right Hon. W. S. Fielding. He allowed a ten per cent preference for freight coming through Canadian ports. I believe that the ten per cent preference should be again allowed in respect of all outgoing freight and at least five per cent for all incoming freight handled through Canadian ports. This would add to employment on the waterfronts; and I advocate, as a measure of fairness and justice to the men engaged there, that the government give serious consideration to setting a floor weekly wage for those who are now known as casual labour. I offer these as constructive suggestions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
My hon. friend has anticipated what is implied in section 6, as giving power to the minister to enable him to perform the duties imposed upon him by the bill. I might mention paragraph (c). The minister may-
. . . consult with representatives of primary producers; industry, science and labour upon any question connected with reconstruction.
The section also mentions the possibility of conferring with other parties. I believe that under that section the minister would) take up immediately" with the Minister of Transport what my hon. friend has suggested, and also confer with labour organizations on the matter to which he has referred. My colleague the Minister of Pensions and National Health has directed my attention to the clause which gives the minister power-
... to coordinate the actions of other departments and agencies of the Government of Canada for the purpose of ensuring that the transition from a war-time to a peace-time economy shall be effected as quickly and as smoothly as possible.
There are apparently several clauses which have been drafted for the purpose of enabling just such steps to tbe considered by the minister as my hon. friend has suggested; and his suggestion is a helpful one.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Establishment of department.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: I assume that the meaning of subsection 3, that such employees as are necessary may be appointed in; the manner authorized by law, means, through the civil service commission?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: That is correct.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-Duties of the minister.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Were it not for the last six words of this section I should look upon this measure as one which provided for the coordination of plans only. But "provide for

Department of Reconstruction
the carrying out thereof" may imply a good deal more than. that. Would the Prime Minister say what he means by the six words?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: Yes. My hon. friend has the correct interpretation. The duty of the minister will be not merely to see that plans are formulated, but to see that such plans as have been framed for the purpose of reconstruction are carried out. The minister will be a member of the cabinet. So far as the plans relate to those made by government departments, I assume he would proceed first of all by consulting his colleague of the department concerned. If that were not adequate to ensure .the carrying out of the plans, he would bring the matter up in cabinet, and the cabinet itself would exercise its collective authority to see that the right steps were taken.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: What would be the relation between this new department and the other departments of government? For instance, the Department of Public Works deals principally with construction. After these years of war, when money has been spent for little other than war purposes, there certainly will be extensions of public buildings, for instance, to mention one thing. I can imagine that the Minister of Public Works might have fairly strong opinions as to what programme should be laid before council and what should be undertaken. Would that programme have to be submitted to the Minister of Reconstruction for his approval before it goes forward to the council?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: I assume the first step the Minister of Reconstruction would take would be to get in touch with every department of government which is undertaking any form of reconstruction work. He would assemble their various projects; he would See, first of all, if there were any overlapping in government departments, whether there was a symmetry about the whole. Any question which was likely to arise, he would take up, in the first instance, with the minister of the department concerned. If there were a difference between them he would bring that matter to the cabinet to be settled there. That would be the method of proceeding.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: The parliamentary committee on reconstruction made two reports to the house and certain specific recommendations of projects across the country. Will these reports be considered by the new minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: Undoubtedly, yes.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Are the recommendations in the reconstruction committee's report to the
house to have any weight, or has the new ministry the authority either to implement or reject them as it sees fit?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: I am sure the minister will welcome, above everything else, any recommendation which comes to him from a committee of parliament. I have no doubt the minister would be the first to recognize that the work which has been done by the committee on reconstruction is just the kind of foundation he requires to begin his work effectively. If it came to a question of whether or not a recommendation should be accepted, someone has to make the final decision. I would say that the minister would be the person who would decide, unless it was some question which should come up to the cabinet as a whole.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Cape Breton South is referring also to the subcommittee reports, the James committee and the Wallace committee, particularly the one on natural resources, which was, I think, an excellent report and should receive careful consideration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: Yes. I believe that, in speaking on the second reading, I took care to refer to these different reports, all of which are exceedingly valuable and practically all of which have been carefully studied already by government officials in the different departments and to a considerable extent by members of the government.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister say how far the jurisdiction would extend in relation to the construction of buildings? Does it extend to the municipalities, or is the extent of a piece of construction governed by the cost?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
The question my hon. friend has asked is, I think, very much to the point. He has just mentioned the construction of buildings by municipalities, and reference has been made to the construction of buildings by the federal government. We may assume that there will also be construction of buildings by provincial governments. Part of the task of the minister-I do not mean actually the minister himself, but his deputies and the experts who are advising him-would be to collect all information possible on what has been done in the construction, for example, of public buildings. If it were found, say, in one community that the municipality intended to construct a building, the province a building, and the federal government a building, part of the duties of the minister would be to call attention to that fact and to say, "Can we
Department of Reconstruction

not in some way see that these three buildings are not put up all at once? We may have a shortage of work later on and we had better reserve this project against such a contingency." That is only an illustration, but the minister's main job would be to apply common sense to the situation which all would be interested in meeting in the most satisfactory way.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: Does it apply to private enterprise or only to public buildings? You cannot construct a building, even a $2,000 building, in a municipality without having first secured a permit from the city clerk or the municipal authorities. Therefore the point is: Is the jurisdiction of the municipality subservient to that of the minister or to this section of the bill? It seems far-fetched surely that this federal government is going to the municipalities to say whether a man shall put up a building or not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: My hon. friend has entirely misunderstood my view if that is the interpretation he puts upon what I have said. The municipality itself, I believe, would welcome all the information it could get with regard, for example, to public buildings to be constructed within its boundaries. The dominion will not invade the jurisdiction of a municipality; it will not invade the jurisdiction of the province. It will give all the assistance it possibly can both to the municipality and to the province with respect to the best way of maintaining employment in the community, not for to-day only but for a period of years.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: I do not care to be persistent, but I should like the Prime Minister to make this clear. Does the federal government invade the jurisdiction of the municipalities in the construction of buildings by private enterprise, or does this section refer only to public buildings? As it stands, it certainly means jurisdiction over the erection of buildings in municipalities, just exactly as it assumes jurisdiction to-day under the building controller. If it does not mean invasion of the jurisdiction of the municipalities, then I think it should certainly be made specific in this clause because one cannot interpret it in any other way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
I think the
word "observation" would be better than the word "jurisdiction" or the term "invasion of jurisdiction." It will be part of the duties of the minister to observe widely what is taking place, but not to seek to enforce jurisdiction on any one. Perhaps what my hon. friend has mostly in mind is this:	Is this an effort
to have the government do things which

private enterprise ought to do? If that is the point, the government would prefer to have private enterprise do whatever it can in the first instance, and it will encourage enterprise as much as possible. But where private enterprise is clearly not able to provide the needed employment, the government ought to come in and assist in preventing unemployment.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
I hope I shall be forgiven
for being persistent, but I should like to ask whether, in the construction of a block, let us say, it will be necessary to apply to the minister for a permit, or does he relieve himself of all that responsibility? To-day such an application is necessary under war conditions, under the building controller. The minister has before him an application from, let us say, the city of Nelson. Let us take a particular case in point. A man was required by the chief of the fire department or by the city authorities to remove a certain building which had been constructed a number of years before. All right. By so doing the city loses taxes on that building; it loses revenue from taxation. At the same time, the owner is saddled with about $250 annually of taxes on property from which he receives no revenue. He arranged with the two adjoining buildings to use the fire walls of each building. In order to secure supplies he tore down an old mining building to obtain the necessary steel beams and the necessary heavy timbers and joists, but he has to come to this department to secure a permit to reconstruct that building under such conditions. My simple question is:	Under
the terms of this section, must a private citizen in any municipality, large or small, come to the federal government or to the minister for a permit in order to proceed with the construction of a building?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
There is
nothing in this section which imposes that obligation or establishes that jurisdiction. The condition to which the hon. member has referred is one arising out of the war. During the war it has become necessary for the federal government to give priority to war purposes over other civilian requirements when there is a limited supply of materials. But we hope that as soon as the war is over, the restrictions which have been imposed will be gradually removed and that we shall get back to a condition where there will be as little interference as possible with private initiative and enterprise.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
But this applies to post-war conditions and we must accept these clauses as the English language expresses them. It is

Department oj Reconstruction
not made clear whether one will have to apply to the federal government for a permit. If that is the case, why not make it clear?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: The condition to which my hon. friend refers is one that arises out of restrictions imposed for a specific purpose, namely, to meet situations that have developed during the war. There is nothing to be gained by putting in this statute a provision that these particular restrictions will be removed later on. They are imposed by virtue of the War Measures Act. I cannot say at the moment how soon these restrictions can be removed. It may be possible to remove some the day after the armistice; it may be necessary in some cases to wait a little time. But there is nothing in this section that creates any permanent restrictions.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: Is not this the point? This bill does not empower the minister to forbid any piece of construction in a municipality?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: That is correct.

Section agreed to.
On section 5-Duties of the minister.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: I have a few questions with regard to paragraph (a). Reference is made to employment in industry. My first question is: Does this refer to employment of men and women in industrial plants engaged in some way in the production of munitions, or does it refer to men and women in private plants not in any way engaged in producing munitions as coming under the minister's duty to provide employment?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: As I read the section it first of all emphasizes the importance of the minister giving his attention to the members of the armed forces and those who are engaged in war industries. That is the purpose of the section.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: Does that apply to plants not engaged in war work?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: That particular section does not apply to them, but the general purpose of the minister would be to seek to further full employment in industry generally. To that extent it is part of the minister's business to get as much information as he can that will help towards that end.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Paragraph (c) of section 5 reads:
to formulate plans for industrial development and conversion. . . .
In carrying out his duties would the minister be able to initiate programmes such as obtained in England prior to the beginning of the war when the British government by regulation insisted on the necessity of fifty per cent British content in any goods imported into England for exportation to Europe, or any goods made in England for exportation to Europe. Would the minister have anything to do with making a regulation like that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: I think that would be a matter of government policy as to the extent of assistance to be given to industry and the like. That would be a matter of policy to be settled by the government. The reference here is to formulating plans for industrial development and conversion. The emphasis is rather on the general policy of bringing forward different projects for new developments or civilian uses for war plants, with a view to having them carried out. There is nothing to prevent the minister from making a recommendation such as my hon. friend has mentioned, but the paragraph does not impose on the minister any obligation of the kind.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: That is a fair answer. The paragraph refers to formulating plans for industrial development. Would that enable the minister to surround himself with capable industrial advisers to inaugurate new lines of manufacturing by making a survey of what we now import with a view of ascertaining if some or all those lines could be manufactured in Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Yes. I think the next section answers my hon. friend's question as -to how he might go about it. The explanatory note refers to powers of the minister. The section reads:
The minister, to enable him to .perform the duties imposed upon him by this act, may: . . .
And then paragraph (e) is as follows:
inaugurate conferences of representatives of primary producers, industry, science and labour as well as representatives of dominion, provin-' cial and municipal authorities engaged or likely to engage in any reconstruction plan.
The minister can bring together any experts he believes will be helpful to him, whether they are individual experts or representatives of industry or officers of industrial establishments, and get their advice with relation to plans for industrial development.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Under paragraph (c)
would the minister have power to consider and perhaps order, as a means of giving vast employment, the initiating of works such as a canal around the Fort Vermilion rapids on

Department of Reconstruction

the Peace river and again around the Fort Fitzgerald and Fort Smith rapids on the Slave river, since the elimination of those rapids would permit the free transportation of coal from Hudson Hope on the Peace river right down to Aklavik, and that Canadian coal could be used for the heating of the north country? Would he have the authority to initiate such works as that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: My reply would be that undoubtedly the minister will welcome suggestions from all sources, and particularly from members of parliament, as to where it might be possible to further some national need or purpose by particular industrial or public works projects such as my hon. friend has mentioned. In the case mentioned by my hon. friend, if he were to speak to the minister himself, the minister would then, I assume, confer with the officials of the Department of Public Works, or the Department of Transport, or whatever departments are concerned, and would ask: "Has this project been considered? Here is a matter that ought to be looked into. If it is thought that that particular area is in need of development works, had we not better consider this among others?" I would not say that the minister would be able to get his way all the time, but certainly that would be one of the things which he would wish to bring to the attention of the departments concerned. In the light of the expenditures involved in the whole programme it might be necessary for the minister to weigh those different projects and come to the cabinet and say: "Here are so many. I would strongly recommend that we do a certain amount." He might not recommend the whole. The government policy as a whole would decide on how far it would be possible to go.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
I have in mind northern Alberta. I am not sure that the government of Alberta have assisted but I am sure they would. In northern Alberta there is a movement to develop the vast coal resources at Hudson Hope and to take them by water down the river. They could then come down as far as Peace River town with very little dredging in the river. The construction of the two canals I mentioned would permit them to take the coal right down to Aklavik at the mouth of the Mackenzie river where they certainly need coal and where coal now costs a tremendous sum of money, because it is taken from away to the south of Edmonton by rail up to Waterways and then on down from there another 1,661 miles. I certainly would strongly advise the new minister to consider that as a project. It would create 
a lot of work and help open up that great country.
Section stands.
Progress reported1.
